abstract: First part of the entry on Madeira's climate, presenting Funchal's reputation as a health resort for consumptives and meteorological data on temperature, pressure, humidity, rainfall and cloud for Funchal, the uplands and Porto Santo.

chapters.title_pt: O clima do Funchal e a tísica
chapters.summary: Physicians since 1751 have praised Funchal's climate for treating pulmonary tuberculosis. The author rejects Dr Mason's criticism and explains the frequency of tuberculosis among locals by alcoholism and poverty.
Funchal has mild, stable temperatures averaging about 18 °C in 1901–1909. Figures are also given for Machico, Santo António da Serra, Poiso, Areeiro and Porto Santo, plus solar radiation readings.
Monthly pressure and humidity averages from the São Lourenço station and other places are given. Humidity is invisible in Funchal, fogs form at 700–1000 m, and dry east winds bring very low humidity.
Rain falls mostly October to April in Funchal, with dry summers; averages and extremes for 1901–1909 are listed. Snow and hail occur in the uplands, and skies are often partly cloudy.

chapters.title_en: Daily weather cycle and mountain fogs
chapters.summary: Mornings bring clouds over the sea that the sea breeze pushes inland, while afternoon north winds clear them and leave starry nights. Mountain fogs come from vapour carried up the slopes by day and often vanish at dusk; in summer they form lower than in winter.

abstract: First part of the entry on the captains-donatary of Madeira, Porto Santo and Machico, describing the origin of the three captaincies, the broad civil and criminal powers granted by the donation charters, and their gradual curtailment by the Crown from 1497 onwards.

chapters.title_en: Origins and powers of the captaincies
chapters.summary: Explains how the archipelago was divided into three captaincies headed by captains-donatary with near-sovereign powers. It sets out why the Funchal captains came to dominate the others.
Quotes the charter granted to João Gonçalves Zarco and summarises the rights it gave: jurisdiction, mills, ovens, salt monopoly and a tenth of revenues.
Describes how the Crown reduced the captains' powers, notably by the 1497 charter making Madeira Crown land, the dispatch of corregedores, and later royal decrees.

chapters.title_en: Decline and abolition of the donataries' powers
chapters.summary: Under Spanish rule the donataries left the island and governed through ouvidores, keeping only their revenues. Pombal turned the captaincies into alcaidarias-mores in 1766, compensating the Count of Castelo Melhor. The alcaidarias were abolished by decree in 1832.

part_abstracts: First part of the entry on the captains-donatary of Madeira, Porto Santo and Machico, describing the origin of the three captaincies, the broad civil and criminal powers granted by the donation charters, and their gradual curtailment by the Crown from 1497 onwards.

This second part traces the decline of the captain-donataries' powers from the Philippine period to Pombal's conversion of the captaincies into alcaidarias-mores and their final abolition in 1832. It closes with lists of the donataries of Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo.

abstract: The Santa Casa da Misericórdia of Santa Cruz, a charitable brotherhood founded in the early sixteenth century whose hospital building dates from 1520, is the most important institution of its kind in Madeira outside Funchal. The entry transcribes a 1920 official report on its building, repairs, finances, staff and patients.

chapters.summary: The Misericórdia was founded in the early 16th century and its hospital built in 1520. It was repaired several times, and in 1920 it still cared for poor patients, although its income was very small.

Its statutes were approved in 1889, and Franciscan hospitaller sisters ran the hospital until their service was ended. It was then run by an elected board. The figures for 1913 show its modest income, its staff and only 14 patients.

abstract: Describes the penitential processions formerly held in Madeira, in which hooded penitents carried images, heavy loads and flogged themselves, usually to pray for rain or other favours. It records the last such rigorous procession in Funchal, with the image of Nossa Senhora do Monte, and the milder survivals of the custom.

chapters.summary: A foreign account of 1819 describes penitents in blue hoods carrying images, stones and chains and whipping themselves. The last rigorous procession in Funchal took the Monte image out during a drought, and rain reportedly fell on its return. Only barefoot women penitents remained in later Passos and Good Friday processions.

abstract: First part of the entry on the geology of the Madeira archipelago, describing its Miocene volcanic origin, the central eruptive focus at Curral das Freiras, and the main rock types and volcanic products (basalts, trachytes, essexites, dykes, tuffs, ashes, clays, limestones) with their local names and building uses.

chapters.summary: The islands rose from the sea in the Miocene through volcanic activity centred on Curral das Freiras. Successive basaltic, trachytic and later eruptions shaped the central mountain chain, with the youngest cones at the island's ends and on the south coast.
Describes basalt forms and their use as building stone, trachytes, trachydolerites and essexites, including the rock Gagel named madeirite.

chapters.title_en: Dykes, lava channels, bombs, tuffs, scoria and ash
chapters.summary: Explains dykes such as the Homem em Pé, lava tubes, volcanic bombs, soft tuff stones, scoria, volcanic ash sands and pumice, and their practical uses.
Covers clays and soils like massapez and salão, seasonal lagoons in old craters, limestone deposits worked for lime, and the calcareous concretions of Piedade and Mornos.
Rain, torrents and the sea have worn down the islands, carved the valleys and changed the coastline. Historical examples show the north coast retreating and the south coast growing.
Landslides create fajãs such as Lugar de Baixo, enlarged by the 1803 flood. Sands take their colour from the rocks they come from, and a 1940 study of the Selvagens' geology is noted.

abstract: First part of the Elucidário's account of the settlement and colonisation of Madeira from about 1425: the division into captaincies, the first settlers and slaves, forest clearing, levadas, sesmarias, the creation of the first parishes and the powers of the captain-donataries.

chapters.summary: The first settlers explored the coast, named places and faced isolation. The island was split into the captaincies of Machico and Funchal, and settlers of all classes, convicts and slaves arrived.
A great fire cleared the forest, levadas were built and land was granted in sesmarias. Slaves did much of the work, entails spread, and a 1460 charter dates settlement to about 1425.
Franciscans served the first chapels, which became parishes. Funchal's parish moved between churches and the town became a vila around 1451–52.
The donataries held near-absolute civil and criminal jurisdiction, exercised through ouvidores and alcaides. Madeira kept special laws until 1834.

chapters.title_en: Early regulations and charters of settlement
chapters.summary: Prince Henry gave the first captains instructions and distributed land by sesmarias, which were forfeited if not farmed within five years. The royal charters of 1433 and the donation letters of 1440–1450 are the oldest known administrative documents. The author notes that these pages come from his 1943 newspaper articles.

abstract: Account of Madeira under Spanish (Philippine) rule, 1580–1640, stressing lawlessness, unpaid troops and clergy, fiscal extortion and the creation of the office of governor-general. It explains why the island readily joined the Restoration of 1640.

chapters.summary: Madeira accepted Spanish rule without resistance. Frutuoso records naval episodes and defence measures, and a patriotic friar was hanged for supporting the Prior of Crato.
Riots and murders plagued Funchal; royal judges were sent in 1614 and 1627, but the governor-general sheltered criminals until censured.

An Inquisition visitor came, Porto Santo was sacked, forts were built and the governor-general post created. Unpaid troops mutinied, the bishop excommunicated officials, and levies led islanders to embrace the 1640 Restoration.

abstract: Part one of the entry on Madeira's parliamentary representation, tracing the island's seat in the old Cortes from 1645 and listing the deputies, senators and elective peers returned for the archipelago from the liberal revolution of 1820 to 1901.

chapters.title_en: Representation in the old Cortes and early liberal period
chapters.summary: Madeira received a seat in the Cortes in 1645, reportedly because it was the first possession to acclaim João IV. After 1820 the island elected deputies to the constitutional assemblies, interrupted by absolutist restorations until 1834.
Lists the deputies and senators elected for Madeira in each legislature from 1834 to 1859, with the decrees dissolving parliament and calling elections.
Lists the deputies elected by the Funchal, Calheta, Santa Cruz and Ponta do Sol constituencies; from 1874 elections were held on the same day as on the mainland.
Lists deputies and elective peers from 1882 to 1901, including Manuel de Arriaga's election for Funchal in 1882.
Records the dissolutions and elections from 1901 to 1910, including two contested elections of Captain João Augusto Pereira. The 1910 parliament never met because the Republic was proclaimed.
Lists Madeira's deputies and senators under the First Republic from 1911, and its deputies and procurador from 1935 to 1946.

abstract: This first part traces the history of the Funchal hospital and the Santa Casa da Misericórdia, from Zargo's land grant of 1454 through the successive hospital buildings, royal privileges and statutes, to the change from confraternity to administrative commissions in 1834. It also covers proposals of 1910–1922 to move the hospital to Santa Clara or Louros.

chapters.summary: Zargo gave land for a hospital in 1454; it moved to Santa Maria Maior around 1484, and D. Manuel ordered a new hospital in 1507. The Misericórdia repeatedly petitioned the kings for a better building.

chapters.title_en: The building on the Terreiro da Sé
chapters.title_pt: O hospital do Terreiro da Sé
chapters.summary: Land on the Terreiro da Sé was leased in 1685 and slow construction began after 1686, helped by royal grants. Inscriptions record new entrances in 1788, 1790 and 1807, and a British infirmary existed in the early nineteenth century.
Doctors recommended building a new hospital on the Santa Clara convent site, which was granted by decrees of 1912 and 1913. In 1922 the Santa Casa asked instead for land at Louros.

chapters.title_en: The confraternity, its privileges and statutes
chapters.summary: The confraternity was founded in 1514 and received many privileges and statutes, notably those of 1631 and 1801. It governed until 1834, after which administrative commissions took over; it was briefly restored in 1906 and dissolved again under the Republic.
After 1834 the Misericórdia was run by administrative commissions under successive regulations. Several attempts to restore the old confraternity failed until a decree of 1906 re-established it.
The institution's finances worsened after 1834 and recovered by 1872. The banker Henrique Vieira de Castro offered a large gift, later refused, and led a public subscription from 1922.

In 1928 the government ceded the Marmeleiros sanatorium to the Misericórdia, and the hospital moved there in 1931 from Santa Isabel. Further improvements were inaugurated in 1940, and the article ends by naming benefactors.

chapters.title_pt: Escritos sobre a Misericórdia do Funchal
chapters.summary: Mentions the orphans' home and the medical school attached to the Funchal hospital. Lists printed regulations, reports and pamphlets on the Misericórdia and its hospital from 1816 to 1933.

Misericórdias also existed at Calheta, Machico, Santa Cruz and Porto Santo, and in 1815 they successfully resisted Funchal's attempt to take over their property. The Calheta house, founded in 1535, housed invalid and incurable people, declined over time, and was restored around 1921.

part_abstracts: This first part traces the history of the Funchal hospital and the Santa Casa da Misericórdia, from Zargo's land grant of 1454 through the successive hospital buildings, royal privileges and statutes, to the change from confraternity to administrative commissions in 1834. It also covers proposals of 1910–1922 to move the hospital to Santa Clara or Louros.

This part traces the administration of the Santa Casa da Misericórdia do Funchal from 1834 to the 1940s: the long rule of appointed administrative commissions, the restoration of the confraternity in 1906, its finances, and the move of the hospital to the former Marmeleiros sanatorium. It also records the main benefactors and administrators of the institution.

This final part lists printed sources on the history of the Misericórdia do Funchal and its Hospital de Santa Isabel, then turns to the smaller rural Misericórdias, chiefly that of Calheta, founded in 1535, which cared for invalid and incurable poor people.

abstract: Opening part of the long entry on Madeira's levadas (irrigation channels), explaining their origin in the needs of the first settlers and their central importance to Madeiran agriculture and to feeding a dense, growing population.

chapters.summary: The first settlers faced dense forest and rugged terrain, with most springs high in the mountains. To irrigate the fertile coastal slopes for vines and sugar cane they built channels called levadas, a centuries-long effort marked by disputes, lawsuits and laws.

Levadas are narrow masonry channels, sometimes tens of kilometres long, that carry water from the central uplands to the farmland. They underpin the island's economy, and irrigation is presented as a remedy for Madeira's very high and rising population density, with new decrees of 1943 promising progress.
Levada flows vary with their springs and are divided into branches. Measurements from 1911 and 1943 give typical flows, and losses come from poor forest cover, theft of water and illegal 'sacadas'.
Irrigation follows a fixed rotation called the giro, usually of 15–20 days. State levadas run from 1 May to 30 September, and water owners are called heréus.

Private levadas were run by a Juiz da Levada elected by the heréus, and later by elected committees after the Civil Code of 1868 and the law of 1888. The Liga das Levadas was founded in 1903, and the state levadas were run by public works and later the Junta Geral.

Early farming on the coast soon needed water brought from far away, so levada building began soon after settlement and continued for five centuries. The oldest irrigated lands were probably along the Santa Luzia, Machico and Câmara de Lobos streams.

Frutuoso describes the dangerous building of the Socorridos levada for Luís de Noronha's sugar mill, with workers hanging in baskets from cliffs, and a costly levada to Machico and Caniçal begun by Rafael Catanho. An 1813 report notes the high cost of levadas.

Royal letters from 1461 onwards denied private owners rights over springs so that water served cultivated land. The Civil Code of 1867 caused lawsuits against levadas, partly remedied by the 1914 law and fully by the decree of 1931.

chapters.title_en: The 1914 law on levada water rights
chapters.summary: The 1914 law confirmed the rights levadas held over springs on other people's land when the Civil Code was published. It also allowed landowners to open new springs, provided the levada's water was measured and protected.

chapters.title_pt: O decreto de 14 de Fevereiro de 1931
chapters.summary: The preamble explains how levadas arose from Madeira's relief and how old royal law denied landowners any right to springs feeding them. It then describes how the Civil Code led to lawsuits and to the remedial law of 1914.

chapters.title_en: Articles of the 1931 decree and further sources
chapters.summary: After the 1919 water law created new risks, the 1931 decree reaffirmed the levadas' rights, including access along their channels. The text also mentions the 1943 decree and Guilherme Moreira's legal study of Madeiran water rights.

chapters.title_en: Proposals to concede or sell the state levadas
chapters.summary: From 1882 onwards several private groups and engineers proposed to finish and run the state levadas. A concession was granted to Captain Manuel Alexandre de Sousa in 1896, but it was cancelled in 1899 without any work having been done. Later bills to sell the levadas, in 1898, 1910 and 1916, all failed.
Madeira has about two hundred levadas, and the largest, such as the Rabaçal, belong to the State. The most important private ones are in Funchal. A list of levadas arranged by parish follows.
Early levadas were built by private cultivators, but larger schemes needed the State. For about a century the government has built and run the main levadas, which are listed here.
Rabaçal lies at the head of the Ribeira da Janela. Surveys were ordered in 1768 and a route was set out in 1835, while further proposals were made in 1819 and 1830.

Work began in 1835 under Mousinho de Albuquerque and sped up under Silvestre Ribeiro. Water first passed through the Estrebarias tunnel in 1855. The old and new levadas cost almost 186 contos in total and irrigate the western Calheta parishes.

The Serra do Faial levada, the longest state levada after Rabaçal, carries water about thirty kilometres to irrigate Caniço, São Gonçalo and Santa Maria Maior. A private company failed to build it in the 1830s–40s. The state began studies in 1861 and inaugurated the levada in 1905.

This chapter describes the state's other levadas: Ribeiro Frio, Juncal, Serra de São Jorge, São Vicente and Ribeira Brava, and Ribeira do Inferno. It also covers recent works by the Junta Geral and the unfinished Coquim levada.

Private levadas date from the first settlement and served mainly sugar cane. The chapter covers the Santa Luzia levada, protected by a royal charter of 1515, and the Piornais levada. It also discusses 1562–63 charters on cleaning levadas and the D. Isabel, Bom Sucesso and Moinhos levadas.

chapters.title_pt: Levada dos Moinhos e nascentes dos Tornos
chapters.summary: Describes how the Levada dos Moinhos water was divided between cleaning Funchal and irrigation in 1855. It also covers the dispute between the Câmara and the Levada de Santa Luzia over the Tornos springs, settled by an agreement in 1912 on the advice of engineers.

chapters.title_en: The waters of the Paul da Serra
chapters.title_pt: As Águas do Paul da Serra
chapters.summary: The Paul da Serra plateau feeds the island's largest streams and levadas. The Junta Geral built experimental dams there to hold back rainwater and increase the flow of springs.

To ease droughts on Porto Santo, the Junta Geral under João Abel de Freitas built a large channel. It collects runoff from Pico do Castelo and lets it soak into the sandy ground to recharge springs and wells.

chapters.title_pt: XIX – Ainda as Levadas do Estado
chapters.summary: Data from the Junta Geral's public works department give the sources, flows, lengths and irrigation rotations of each state levada in 1943. Rental prices per hour, revenues for 1939–43 and repair spending, including a 1940 surcharge to fund waterproof lining, are also listed.

chapters.title_en: The Technical Mission and Its Reports
chapters.title_pt: XX – A Construção das Novas Levadas
chapters.summary: A 1939 decree sent a technical mission to study hydro-electric and irrigation potential in Madeira. Its reports, completed in late 1941, are summarised, including eighteen proposed schemes on various streams.

chapters.title_en: The 1943 Decrees and the Works Plan
chapters.summary: Decrees 33.158 and 33.159 of October 1943 created an administrative commission and a 60,000-conto ten-year plan, shared equally by the State and the Junta Geral. The works would irrigate 3,111 hectares and supply about 5,830 kW of power.

chapters.title_en: Legal framework for the new levadas
chapters.summary: The rules governing the new state irrigation works are set out: loans, the administrative commission, the land register, irrigators' associations and the charges landowners pay. The rules also cover the sale of hydro-electric power.
This section is a glossary of the traditional Madeiran words for the parts of a levada and for the irrigation system. It explains terms for water owners, officials, charges and watchmen.

chapters.title_pt: XXII – As Levadas e os Arvoredos
chapters.summary: Forests attract rain, hold water in the soil and feed the springs, so levada flows shrink as trees are cut. The author recalls royal decrees protecting the woods from 1493 onwards and urges reforestation of the mountains.
A chronological list of the laws governing levadas from 1451 to 1943, identifying the fundamental ones. It then lists the key studies, pamphlets and newspaper debates on the levadas.

part_abstracts: Opening part of the long entry on Madeira's levadas (irrigation channels), explaining their origin in the needs of the first settlers and their central importance to Madeiran agriculture and to feeding a dense, growing population.

This part of the Levadas entry describes the flow volumes of Madeira's irrigation channels, how irrigation turns (giros) operate, and how the channels were administered, from heir-elected judges to associations and state public works.

This part of the Levadas entry covers the earliest irrigation channels of Madeira, quoting Gaspar Frutuoso on the perilous construction of the Socorridos and Machico levadas, and traces the legislation on water ownership from 1461 to the decree of 1931.

This part covers the legal status of Madeira's levadas, reproducing the law of 20 April 1914 and the decree of 14 February 1931, which restored the levadas' centuries-old rights to springs rising on other people's land after the Civil Code had put them in doubt.

This part of the Levadas entry recounts the failed proposals, from 1882 to 1916, to concede, lease or sell Madeira's state-owned levadas to private operators, including Captain Manuel Alexandre de Sousa's short-lived concession of 1896–99. It then surveys the roughly two hundred existing levadas and lists them parish by parish.

This part covers the state-owned levadas of Madeira and, in particular, the history of the Rabaçal levadas. They were planned from 1768, begun in 1835 under Luís Mousinho de Albuquerque, pushed forward by José Silvestre Ribeiro and finished in 1890, bringing water from the north of the island to the Calheta parishes.

This part of the Levadas entry describes the Levada da Serra do Faial and other state-owned levadas, then begins the account of the oldest private levadas (Santa Luzia, Piornais, D. Isabel, Bom Sucesso, Moinhos), with the royal charters that regulated them in the sixteenth century.

This part of the Levadas entry covers the use and water disputes of the Levada dos Moinhos and Santa Luzia in Funchal, the waters of the Paul da Serra plateau and the Junta Geral's retention works there (1938–40), and the rainwater channel built on Porto Santo in the 1940s.

This part gives 1943 statistics on the state-owned levadas of Madeira (sources, flows, lengths, irrigation rotations, rents, revenues and repair costs), then describes the 1939 technical mission and the 1943 decrees launching a ten-year programme of new irrigation and hydro-electric works.

This part concludes the summary of the 1940s legal framework for the state's new hydro-agricultural works in Madeira (administrative commission, irrigators' associations, charges for improvement and irrigation) and begins a glossary of traditional levada terminology. The glossary covers terms such as madre, mainel, furado, giro, heréu, terral and vigias.

This final part of the Levadas entry explains how forests on the mountains sustain the springs that feed Madeira's irrigation channels, and recalls royal laws against deforestation since 1493. It closes with a list of the main laws and writings on levadas from 1451 to 1943.

History and description of vine-growing in Madeira from the fifteenth century, through the oidium and phylloxera crises, to the grafted vineyards of the early twentieth century, with descriptions of the main grape varieties. This first part also begins Carlos Azevedo de Meneses's detailed account of the red varieties.

chapters.title_pt: Origem e história da cultura da vinha
chapters.summary: Vines were already grown in Madeira by 1445, when Malvasia was said to have been brought from Crete. Vine-growing expanded after 1640 under English merchants, was devastated by oidium in 1851–52 and phylloxera in 1871–72, and recovered through grafting onto American vines.

Describes trellising, pruning, soils and altitude limits of Madeiran vineyards. The five principal varieties (Malvasia, Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Tinta) and many minor and American varieties are described, with sources for further reading.
Quotes the botanist Carlos Azevedo de Meneses's 1902 article describing red varieties such as Listrão, Tinta da Madeira, Negra Mole, Tinta de Lisboa and Bastardo, with where each is grown.
A botanical description of the Tinta do Porto Santo vine, covering its leaves, bunches and sweet, firm berries with violet pulp. It is a very productive variety that now grows only on Porto Santo.

abstract: This first part of the entry traces the history of the Funchal customs house, from the first royal tax collectors of the fifteenth century and its creation by charter of 15 March 1477 to its officials, fiscal regulations and nineteenth-century reforms. It also describes the Manueline customs building, its redoubt and its chapel of Santo António.

chapters.title_en: Origins and officials of the Funchal customs
chapters.summary: Customs duties began to be collected in Funchal in the mid-fifteenth century, and the customs house was created by royal charter in 1477. The entry lists its judges from 1494 to 1768 and its other offices.

Customs revenues were first farmed out to contractors, and a 1512 decree made Funchal the only port for exporting sugar. Edicts regulated landing goods, and constitutional reforms from 1834 reorganised the customs.

The customs was probably first housed near Rua do Esmeraldo or Rua Direita before the Manueline building still in use. The building was altered in 1733, damaged by the 1748 earthquake, and had a redoubt and a chapel beside it.

Revenue figures for the Madeira customs houses from 1581–1587, 1748, 1812–1840 and 1896–1932 are given. The text notes that currency devaluation makes comparisons difficult, and it adds the municipal taxes collected for the district's eleven councils.
The directors of the Funchal customs house from 1889 onwards are listed. A bibliography follows of pamphlets and regulations concerning the customs, including an unpublished draft regulation of 1824.

It also describes the Manueline customs building, its redoubt and its chapel of Santo António.

abstract: History of policing and public security in Funchal from the alcaides and quadrilheiros of the fifteenth century to the civil police of the 1920s and 1930s. It traces successive reorganisations and the author's criticism of the inadequate policing of the city in 1921.

chapters.summary: Early security in Funchal rested on the alcaide and ward officers called quadrilheiros, with a curfew bell. Disorder persisted, especially under Spanish rule, and visitors in 1687 and 1689 saw citizens carrying weapons.

chapters.title_en: From military patrols to liberal reforms
chapters.summary: Night patrols by militia and soldiers were requested in 1812–1826. Under the Miguelist governor the quadrilheiros persecuted liberals, and after 1834 new police posts were created under the Provedor and the Administrador do Concelho.
Reorganisations from 1856 to 1894 created a police chief, then a commissioner post and a force of 50 guards in two stations, still in place in 1921.
The author judged Funchal poorly policed in 1921; the Republican Guard sent in 1919 caused conflicts and left in 1922. The police moved into a building in Rua da Carreira in 1934.

abstract: Survey of agriculture in the Madeira archipelago, its main occupation: the extent of arable land, four altitude-based agricultural zones, farming methods, and the three 'rich crops' of sugar cane, vine and banana, with wine production figures for 1910–1930.

chapters.summary: About three quarters of Madeirans farm roughly 30,000 hectares of arable land. Following Carlos Azevedo de Meneses, the island is divided into four altitude zones, each with typical crops, from subtropical sugar cane and bananas on the coast to uncultivated peaks.

abstract: Entry on sheep farming in Madeira and Porto Santo, reproducing an article by the agricultural engineer Torres Baptista on flock numbers, the poor quality of local wool and proposals to improve breeds for wool or milk.

chapters.title_en: Pastures and the livestock of the islands
chapters.summary: The editors introduce Torres Baptista's article. He contrasts Madeira's acid pastures, suited to milk, with Porto Santo's limestone pastures, which produce sturdy animals. He counts about 16,000 sheep on Madeira and 600 on Porto Santo, and argues that meat production is not a priority.

chapters.title_en: Wool or milk: proposals for improvement
chapters.title_pt: Lã ou leite: melhoria das raças
chapters.summary: He recommends breeding for wool on Porto Santo, and for either milk (for cheese) or wool on Madeira, using merino, Alentejo black, Larzac or saloia breeds. He also proposes summer grazing in the uplands. Local wool is so coarse that it is fit only for mattresses and rough goods.

abstract: The Mosteiro Novo was an unfinished convent begun in Funchal by Canon Manuel Afonso Rocha in the 17th century, whose building later housed the Diocesan Seminary for most of the period from 1697 to 1909 and again after 1911.

chapters.summary: Canon Manuel Afonso Rocha began a monastery dedicated to São José but never finished it. In 1638 he placed it under the bishop's care, and it was later lived in by his nephews and nieces.

chapters.summary: Above 150–200 metres lie the middle-zone meadows on ravine sides and hills, and above 750–800 metres the mountain pastures. Rare fine forage plants such as Festuca albida grow in the Ribeira da Metade and Boaventura ravines.

chapters.summary: The convent was founded by João Gonçalves da Câmara next to the church built by Zarco, endowed with the Curral estate. Building ran from 1492 to 1497, and the founder's descendants claimed patronage and ownership.

The convent's income and property sale, the death of the last nun in 1890, and the successive twentieth-century grants of the buildings to the Franciscan Missionaries of Mary, the municipality and charities.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Fajã da Ovelha in the municipality of Calheta, western Madeira. It discusses the origin of the parish name, the parish's founding from the chapel of São Lourenço and the building of its new church in the 18th century, and lists its localities, streams, levadas and notable natives.

chapters.title_en: Name and origins of the parish
chapters.summary: The author argues that the parish was always called Fajã da Ovelha, as a document of 1553 already uses the name. The parish grew from the old chapel of São Lourenço, whose last chaplain became its first parish priest.

The curacy existed before 1553 and became an independent parish shortly before 1573. A new church was authorised in 1705 and contracted out in 1747. Ponta do Pargo and Prazeres were later separated from the parish.

The entry lists the main localities, streams and levadas, and mentions manganese ore found in the parish. It also gives the population, schools and medical district, and names notable people born there.

abstract: The Madeiran osier or willow, a probable hybrid of Salix alba and S. fragilis, whose flexible shoots supply the island's wickerwork industry. The entry describes its cultivation, the export trade in raw and worked wicker, and the causes of the industry's decline around 1921.

chapters.summary: The Madeiran osier exists only as female plants and is propagated from cuttings. Its shoots are used for furniture, baskets and ties, and large quantities of raw and worked wicker were exported in 1912.

Wickerwork began at Camacha around 1850 but was declining by 1921 because of costly raw material, emigration of workers, freight costs and taxes. Osiers are pruned from January to March and peeled after sprouting, and Camacha and Boaventura are the main producing places.

abstract: A discussion rejecting the Danish botanist Martin Vahl's classification of the dry lowland vegetation of Madeira, dominated by Andropogon hirtum, as steppe. chapters.summary: Martin Vahl classed Madeira's dry lowland grass vegetation as steppe. The Elucidário disagrees, pointing to the constant water vapour from the nearby sea, which soils and plants can absorb.

abstract: First part of the entry on Madeira's wine industry, tracing wine production and export from the fifteenth century to the 1930s, the dominance of British merchants, the oidium and phylloxera crises, and the persistent problem of adulteration and counterfeiting.

chapters.summary: Madeira produced wine soon after settlement, and exports are recorded from the sixteenth century. Large-scale trade began after 1660, driven by English merchants and barter with visiting ships.

Figures show exports rising to about 20,000 pipes early in the nineteenth century, then falling with disease. Twentieth-century figures and foreign markets, including the French ban of 1923, are given.
War-time demand was followed by decline caused by adulteration and competition from other wines. Decrees, municipal ordinances and vintage inspectors tried to protect quality.

British merchants came to control prices, harming growers until oidium in 1852 drove most of them away. Phylloxera and later fraud hurt the trade, and international treaties are urged against false labelling.
Describes abuses in the use of alcohol, lists the wine exporters of 1921, and gives production figures showing the collapse after disease and recovery after grafting.
Describes malvasia, boal, sercial, verdelho, tinta, Madeira and vinho surdo, and gives historical prices per pipe.
Explains the vintage, treading, pressing, fermentation, clarification, heating and fortification, then the 1913 regulation, later reforms and a bibliography.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Ribeira da Janela on the north-west coast of Madeira, named after the stream and the islet with a window-like hole near its mouth. It covers the parish's origins, the history of its church and curacy, the scenery of its uplands including Fanal, its irrigation, localities and population.

chapters.summary: The parish takes its name from the stream, itself named after an islet with a window-like hole. Its land once belonged mostly to Porto Moniz and partly to Seixal, and there were settlers by the mid-16th century.

The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação was built by the people, probably in 1699, enlarged in 1754 and turned into a full church by 1874–79. A curacy was created in 1726–33 and later became an independent parish.
The uplands, especially Fanal, are famed for their beauty. The fertile land is watered by levadas; the entry lists the main localities and gives 748 inhabitants in 1921.

abstract: First part of the entry on the discovery of the Madeira archipelago, reviewing legends of earlier voyages and the chroniclers' accounts of Zarco and Tristão Vaz reaching Porto Santo and then Madeira, with debate over the exact date (traditionally 1–2 July 1419). It ends by noting that later research suggests the islands were already known to Portuguese navigators before that date.

chapters.title_en: Importance of the question and ancient legends
chapters.summary: The discovery of Madeira marks the start of Portuguese maritime expansion, yet its date is uncertain. Legends of Atlantis, Saint Brendan, ancient voyagers and a 14th-century Spanish friar are reviewed and generally rejected.

According to Azurara, a storm drove Zarco and Tristão Vaz to Porto Santo while seeking Guinea, and they then crossed to Madeira. Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo's commentary and the later chroniclers support this account.

Frutuoso dates the sighting to Sunday 1 July and landing 2 July 1419, but Manuel Sardinha showed that 2 July 1419 was the Sunday. The author concludes the landing at Machico was on Sunday 2 July 1419.
Later studies question the traditional dates and suggest the islands were already known to Portuguese sailors, with secrecy surrounding early voyages.

The royal charters say nothing of a discovery, suggesting Zarco and Tristão Vaz only reconnoitred islands already known. A bibliography of studies follows. The author concludes the islands were known before 1418, reconnoitred about 1418–1425 and settled from about 1425.

part_abstracts: First part of the entry on the discovery of the Madeira archipelago, reviewing legends of earlier voyages and the chroniclers' accounts of Zarco and Tristão Vaz reaching Porto Santo and then Madeira, with debate over the exact date (traditionally 1–2 July 1419). abstract: Describes two civic-religious processions in Funchal: the procession of the Bull of the Holy Crusade, held in the early nineteenth century, and the votive procession of 1 May in honour of São Tiago, the city's patron saint. chapters.summary: Moniz was born in Funchal in 1837, studied law at Coimbra with top honours, and became famous for defending the deputy Vieira de Castro in a celebrated murder trial before abandoning the bar.

abstract: History of the municipal councils of Madeira, chiefly the Senado da Câmara of Funchal, from the fifteenth-century council of 'homens bons' to the republican municipal laws of 1913 and 1916. It covers composition, elections, ceremonial precedence and officials.

chapters.summary: From 1470 the Funchal council was made up of 'homens bons', with craft representatives, a presiding judge and a procurator. Royal regulations of 1505 and 1508 fixed its officers and restricted councillorships to noblemen, and officers were chosen by lot from wax balls.

The council kept four councillors, later named by the Desembargo do Paço, and was presided over by the juiz de fora from the mid-seventeenth century. Seating rules kept the mesteres apart, causing a dispute in 1803, and a 1763 charter set its place in the Corpus Christi procession.

chapters.title_pt: As câmaras no regime liberal e republicano
chapters.summary: The first liberal municipal elections took place in 1835, and successive administrative codes and the laws of 1913 and 1916 changed the number of councillors. The Republic restored municipal freedoms by reviving the decentralising code of 1878.

chapters.summary: Mouzinho de Albuquerque began a suspension bridge meant also as a monument to the Duke of Bragança. The work stopped when he left, Lordelo failed to resume it, and José Silvestre Ribeiro revived it in 1846–48.

abstract: Biography of the Scottish physician Robert Reid Kalley (1809–1888), who lived in Funchal from 1838 to 1846, gained fame for free medical care and schools, and then for Protestant proselytism that ended with the riot of 9 August 1846 and his flight from Madeira. It also covers the diplomatic claim for compensation, settled by Portugal in 1853.

chapters.summary: Kalley, born near Glasgow in 1809, qualified in medicine and arrived in Funchal in 1838. He first won respect for free medical care, charity and schools, but after a visit to England in 1845 turned to intense Protestant propaganda.

His preaching provoked conflict; on 9 August 1846 a crowd sacked his house at Vale Formoso and he escaped disguised as a woman. He went to Illinois, followers emigrated, and Lisbon sent António José de Ávila to investigate.

Through the British government Kalley claimed damages, and Portugal paid 1,574 pounds (about seven contos) after reports by José Silvestre Ribeiro. Pamphlets on the affair and the 1853 report of the Visconde de Atouguia are cited.

Biography of Joaquim José Ferreira de Freitas, a Madeiran-born adventurer, journalist and pamphleteer known as 'Padre Amaro' after the London periodical he published in support of Portuguese liberalism. He died in London in 1831.

abstract: History of the town and municipality of Santa Cruz in eastern Madeira, raised to a vila in 1515 within the captaincy of Machico, with its customs house, Misericórdia, rivalry with Machico and later boundary changes.

abstract: First part of the Elucidário's account of sport in Madeira, covering the early football clubs and championships of the Associação de Foot-ball do Funchal, notable Madeiran sportsmen in tennis, diving, water-polo, billiards and sailing, and the origins of cricket and football on the island from 1865 onwards.

chapters.title_pt: O foot-ball e o Campeonato da Madeira
chapters.summary: A sports journalist describes the sports played in Madeira and the two phases of football there. The Associação de Foot-ball do Funchal was founded in 1916 and organised the Madeira Championship, which Club Sport Marítimo dominated.
Madeiran players who excelled in lawn tennis, high diving, water-polo, billiards, table tennis and sailing are named.
Histories are given of Club Sport Marítimo, Grupo Sportivo Internacional, Club Sports da Madeira and the nautical sports league, including notable matches against Benfica, FC Porto and Sporting.

A supplement for the second edition begins with cricket, introduced by British residents, organised from 1888 at the Achada da Camacha and later played at Campo do Brás, until it died out around 1926.

Harry Hinton brought the first football to Madeira in 1865. The first organised match took place in 1894 or 1895 on the Campo D. Carlos, and the game grew between 1908 and 1910 thanks to Humberto dos Passos Freitas.

Madeiran football reached its peak when Marítimo won the Championship of Portugal in 1926. The text lists championship results, inter-city matches, clubs and famous players such as Pinga, before noting a later decline caused by players leaving and a lack of pitches.
Nautical festivals, the Club Naval Madeirense (1917) and swimming and water-polo bodies are described, followed by the modest history of athletics, including marathons to Câmara de Lobos.
Tennis was popular among the elite and was played by King Carlos in 1901. Fencing, table tennis, motoring from the first car in 1903, cycling, basketball and volleyball are then briefly chronicled.

abstract: History of the Madeiran dairy industry, chiefly butter making, from rudimentary production to the factories and skimming stations of the early twentieth century, with prices, exports, public supply rules and the 1936 creation of the Junta Nacional de Lacticínios da Madeira, which provoked rural unrest.

The industry kept growing after 1921, and a 1936 decree created the Junta Nacional de Lacticínios da Madeira. Rural protests against the decrees were suppressed by troops, with deaths and deportations.

abstract: Entry on the birch (vidoeiro), quoting the botanist Carlos de Meneses, who argued that birches sent to Porto Santo in 1910 were unsuitable for reafforesting that dry island. He recommended evergreen Madeiran or Mediterranean trees instead.

chapters.summary: Birches were sent to Porto Santo in 1910 for reafforestation. Carlos de Meneses argued that only Madeiran or Mediterranean trees suit the island, and that even the vinhático would eventually fail there.

Porto Santo's dry, warm climate suits only lowland species such as the laurel, til and barbusano. The deciduous northern birch is wholly unsuitable, because evergreen cover is needed to protect the soil and encourage springs.

abstract: History of Freemasonry in Madeira from the first lodge known in 1770, through the persecutions of 1792, 1823 and 1828, to the lodges active in Funchal in 1921.

chapters.summary: Lodges existed in Madeira by 1770, and the Frenchman Orquiny founded another after 1789. Bishop Costa Torres prompted an Inquisition edict in 1792, which led to arrests and flight until the government issued a pardon.
Victims of the persecution protested and the bishop left the island. Freemasonry revived under the British occupations, but was dispersed by the absolutist inquiries of 1823 and 1828.
After decades with no lodge, the Liberdade lodge was founded in 1872 and others followed. By 1921 several lodges were active in Funchal, including an English one.

abstract: Biography of Dr João Francisco de Oliveira (1761–1829), a Funchal-born physician to the royal court who staged the abduction of D. Eugénia de Meneses to shield the Prince Regent, and later served as diplomat, minister and deputy for Madeira. The entry also covers his benefactions in Funchal and the fate of his estates.

chapters.summary: Born in Funchal in 1761, Oliveira took his doctorate in medicine at Coimbra and then practised in Lisbon. He became physician to the royal palace and chief physician of the army, and enjoyed the favour of the Prince Regent, the future D. João VI.

chapters.title_pt: O rapto de D. Eugénia de Meneses
chapters.summary: He staged the abduction of a lady-in-waiting, D. Eugénia de Meneses, to spare the Prince Regent a scandal. He was sentenced to death and practised medicine in the United States, and was later acquitted in Rio de Janeiro in 1820.
He served as Portugal's envoy in London and Paris, and was a minister briefly in 1823. As deputy for Madeira he proposed a bank, a wine-export company and a new quay in Funchal.

Back in Funchal he was provedor of the Misericórdia and founded a surgery class at the Santa Isabel hospital; he died in Lisbon in 1829. His estates passed to his children, and his daughter's inheritance later paid for building the Seminário da Incarnação.

abstract: Account of the vegetation of Porto Santo, quoted from a 1908 study by the botanist Carlos de Meneses, covering phylloxera damage to vines, fruit trees, native and introduced woody species, and the island's flora statistics and useful plants.

chapters.summary: The text is taken from a 1908 newspaper study by Carlos de Meneses. Phylloxera has badly damaged Porto Santo's vines, and resistant American vine species are recommended for the island's limestone soils.
Figs and mulberries are the main fruit trees. The original juniper and dragon-tree cover is extinct, only a few native shrubs remain, and several foreign trees have been introduced.
The island has 325 plant species, two of them apparently endemic. Many fodder plants are abundant, and some plants yield soda, fibre for rope, or opium.

abstract: Biography of D. Jerónimo Fernando, ninth bishop of Funchal (appointed 1619, took office 1621, died 1650), nicknamed 'Bravo'. He was a strict reformer who three times acted as interim governor of Madeira.

chapters.summary: Jerónimo Fernando of Santarém was appointed bishop of Funchal in 1619 and took office in 1621. Camilo Castelo Branco tells a story of his illegitimate descent from the Infante D. Fernando.

Nicknamed 'Bravo' for his harsh manner, he reformed church discipline and gave the cathedral a great organ. He was the first bishop to visit Porto Santo and governed the archipelago three times. He left for the mainland in 1641 and died in Lisbon in 1650.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Nossa Senhora do Monte (commonly 'Monte') above Funchal, covering its origin in Adão Gonçalves Ferreira's chapel, the legend of the Virgin's apparition, the building of the church, the island-wide cult and August pilgrimage, and its quintas, railway and toboggans.

chapters.summary: The parish takes its name from a chapel built around 1470 by Adão Gonçalves Ferreira. The entry recounts the legend of the Virgin appearing to a shepherd girl at Terreiro da Luta.

The parish was created in 1565; the old chapel was replaced by a new church built 1741–47, damaged by the 1748 earthquake and consecrated in 1818. Many royal visitors came, and Emperor Charles of Austria was provisionally buried there.

Devotion to Our Lady of Monte grew after 1750 into the island's largest pilgrimage on 14–15 August. After the 1803 flood she was made patroness of the island; early priests and their stipends are listed.
Called the 'Madeiran Sintra', Monte is a fashionable summer resort with fine quintas, a railway, a motor road and wicker toboggans. Plans for a monument to the Virgin are noted.

abstract: First part of the biography of João Gonçalves Zargo, discoverer and first captain-donatary of Funchal: the spelling and origin of his surname, his uncertain birthplace and date, his noble ancestry and marriage, his military and naval career, and his successive residences in Funchal.

chapters.title_en: Significance and the name Zarco or Zargo
chapters.title_pt: O descobridor e o seu apelido
chapters.summary: The discovery of Madeira is presented as Portugal's first great maritime achievement. The entry discusses whether the name should be spelt Zarco or Zargo and reviews legends and genealogical explanations of its origin, including a lost eye at Tangier.
His birthplace is unknown, with Matosinhos the most likely candidate; he was probably born shortly after 1390. He came of noble stock and married Constança Rodrigues de Sá.

Zargo served Prince Henry from youth, sailed the African coast, guarded the Algarve coast and fought at Ceuta and Tangier. In Funchal he lived first near Santa Catarina, then near São Paulo, and finally near the Conceição de Cima church (Quinta das Cruzes).

Zargo colonised his captaincy, whose seat became a town and later a city. The entry describes the great forest fire, the donation charter of 1450 and the donataries' wide powers, and explains why Funchal's captains outweighed those of Machico.
Zargo's wife Constança Rodrigues de Sá, their children and illustrious descendants are described, along with the coat of arms granted in 1460.
The year of Zargo's death is uncertain (1451, 1461 or 1471). He was buried in Santa Clara church, but his tomb was later removed and no trace of it was found in 1919.
Buildings linked to Zargo, his two-handed sword and Francisco Franco's statues are discussed, followed by Medina e Vasconcelos's epic poem Zargueida and a note on corrections.

chapters.summary: The text weighs a 1447 document spelling the name 'Zargo' against the usual 'Zarco' used by Frutuoso and most writers. It notes that João Cabral do Nascimento proved Zargo died in 1467, discusses doubts about his sword given to the Funchal museum by Henrique Hinton, and records the statue unveiled on 28 May 1934.

part_abstracts: First part of the biography of João Gonçalves Zargo, discoverer and first captain-donatary of Funchal: the spelling and origin of his surname, his uncertain birthplace and date, his noble ancestry and marriage, his military and naval career, and his successive residences in Funchal.

This part covers João Gonçalves Zargo's rule as first captain-donatary of Funchal, his powers and privileges, marriage and descendants, coat of arms, uncertain date of death, burial at Santa Clara, surviving relics, planned and existing monuments, and the epic poem Zargueida.

This closing part of the entry on João Gonçalves Zargo discusses whether his surname should be spelt Zargo or Zarco, the establishment of 1467 as the year of his death, the disputed attribution of his two-handed sword (montante), and the inauguration of his statue in Funchal in 1934.

abstract: Reproduces an article by the botanist Carlos Azevedo de Meneses on phenological observations (leafing, leaf fall and winter dormancy) of introduced trees in Funchal and Monte in 1905–1906, compared with earlier data and with Coimbra. It explains Madeira's long dormancy periods by the dry summers and the high heat needed for budding.

chapters.summary: The article's origin is explained and earlier observations by Heer and Meneses are noted. The oak in Funchal leafs extraordinarily early, from December, but much later at Monte.

Dates of leaf colouring and budding are given for horse chestnut, plane, vines, robinia, lime, fig, cherimoya, chestnut and walnut. Dormancy lengths are compared with averages for 1903–1905 and with Coimbra.

Dry Funchal summers cause early leaf fall, and many trees need more accumulated heat to bud than in their native lands. The oak is an exception, and heavy rain in late 1905 probably brought budding forward.

abstract: Explains the sesmaria land grants by which Madeira's donatary captains distributed land to settlers, and argues that the sesmaria gradually evolved into the island's distinctive colonia tenancy contract.

chapters.title_en: Origins and terms of the sesmarias
chapters.summary: The sesmaria laws of King Fernando aimed to make abandoned land productive. In Madeira the donatary captains granted land in sesmaria on five-year conditions of cultivation, and no rent or tax on such grants is known.

Land went to nobles and foreign merchants, worked by African slaves; rich grantees created entailed estates and let the land to free tenants on half shares. The tenants' improvements gave them near co-ownership, which was the origin of the colonia contract.

abstract: History of the Teatro Grande, a large opera house built around 1780 facing the São Lourenço palace in Funchal, reputedly the second-largest theatre in Portugal, and demolished in 1833 under the absolutist government because it had become a venue for liberal demonstrations.

First part of a chronological survey of popular riots and disturbances in Madeira, from the Porto Santo prophets of 1533 to the Machico election violence of 1870, including the 1668 deposition of Governor Francisco de Mascarenhas and the 1868 'Pedrada' riot.

chapters.summary: The islanders are described as peaceful, rioting only when misled. The 1533 Porto Santo prophets and the 1641 popular expulsion of officials after the Restoration are recounted.
Nobles attacked and deposed Governor D. Francisco de Mascarenhas, shipping him to Galicia. A later inquiry condemned several nobles to exile in Angola.
Brief notes on riots over the Paul da Serra, the 1821 Constitution, soldiers' unrest in 1829, the 1834 Calheta events, the 1846 anti-Kalley troubles and 1847.
Political crowds stoned Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos to prevent his landing in Funchal; troops fired and several died. A faked fire dispersed the mob.
Troops fired on a crowd inside Machico church during elections, killing several; further disturbances followed in Funchal.

chapters.title_en: Election riots, the Parreca and the 1894 cholera scare
chapters.summary: Election riots in 1884 left several people shot dead at Ribeira Brava. The 1887–88 Parreca disturbances spread terror across the parishes, and in 1894 crowds stoned troops to stop passengers landing for fear of cholera.

Wild rumours about crimes inside the Gonçalo Aires isolation hospital during a suspected plague outbreak led a crowd to sack it on 7 January 1906. Public anger fell chiefly on Dr Balbino do Rego, and many pamphlets and popular verses followed.
A proposed rise in flour prices led to a general shutdown and riots in Funchal in August 1921. Shortly before, election riots at Câmara de Lobos had injured two election observers.

chapters.title_en: Grain monopoly riots of 1931 and milk riots of 1936
chapters.summary: A decree restricting wheat imports caused violent riots in Funchal in February 1931, with deaths and heavy damage. In August 1936 a decree regulating milk sales provoked rural riots that left eight dead and led to mass arrests.

abstract: History of the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia in Funchal, a hospital for poor sufferers of pulmonary tuberculosis founded by the Empress D. Amélia in memory of her daughter, who died in Madeira in 1853. It covers its provisional opening, the new building (1856–59), its running by the Sisters of Charity, its perpetual endowment by Queen Josefina of Sweden, and its administration, chaplains and physicians.

chapters.summary: After Princess Maria Amélia died in Funchal in 1853, her mother the Empress Amélia founded a hospice for 24 poor consumptives. It opened provisionally in the Rua do Castanheiro in July 1853 under Dr Luz Pita and a committee.

A law of 1853 granted the foundation its privileges. The foundation stone was laid in 1856, the building was finished in 1859, and the first patients were admitted in 1862 under the Sisters of Charity.

The hospice closed in 1862 when the Sisters of Charity were expelled, and reopened in 1871. After the Empress died, Queen Josefina and King Oscar of Sweden made it a perpetual foundation run by a council based in Lisbon.
The chaplains and physicians are listed, and distinguished visitors are noted. An orphanage with schools was added in 1878 but later almost disappeared.

abstract: Entry on Count Giulio Landi, author of a Latin description of Madeira published with an Italian translation by Alemanio Fini at Piacenza in 1574, which the Elucidário shows was plagiarised almost verbatim by Padre Manuel Constantino in his Insulae Materiae Historia. abstract: Account of the patron saints of the diocese and city of Funchal: St James the Less, chosen by lot during the plague of 1521 and honoured by municipal vows, and Our Lady of Monte, adopted as protector after the flood of 1803.

chapters.summary: The diocese has St James the Less as chief patron and St Sebastian and St Roch as lesser patrons. His feast on 1 May was kept for nearly four centuries with a procession from the cathedral to Santa Maria Maior.

During plague and famine in 1521 the council drew lots and St James the Less was chosen patron; a chapel was built and the vow renewed in 1523. The plague of 1538 reportedly ended after the health officer handed his staff to the saint.

chapters.title_en: The auto of 1632 and later revival
chapters.summary: A 1632 deed credited the saint with sparing Madeira from plague, enemy fleets and famine. In 1942 the council revived the homage on 1 May.

abstract: A small chapel of Our Lady, probably dedicated to the Assumption, that stood at the Varadouros, the main landing place on the Funchal beach; rebuilt in 1689 above the city's main gate by Governor D. Lourenço de Almada, it was demolished in April 1911.

chapters.title_pt: Os Varadouros e a reconstrução da capela
chapters.summary: The Varadouros was the main landing place on Funchal's beach, and it gave its name to one of the city's oldest chapels. The original chapel was pulled down around 1682 to open the main city gate. It was rebuilt above the gate's arch in 1689 under Governor Lourenço de Almada, and a Latin inscription recorded his work.

The author regrets that the council demolished the gate and chapel instead of preserving them. Governors and bishops had made their ceremonial entries into the city through this gate. The chapel's altar was moved to a sacristy of the Cathedral, where an English sign wrongly calls it Funchal's first chapel.

abstract: History of the Society of Jesus in Madeira, from the arrival of the first Jesuits after the French sack of Funchal in 1566 and the founding of their college in 1569–70 to their imprisonment and expulsion under Pombal in 1759–60. It also describes their revenues, country residences and the sale of their property.

chapters.summary: Two Jesuits came with the captain-donatary after the 1566 sack of Funchal. King Sebastião founded a college in 1569, and the first community arrived in March 1570 and opened classes in May.
The Jesuits taught Latin, moral theology, logic and rhetoric in the 'Aulas do Pátio'. They held country residences and large revenues from estates and public taxes in several parishes.
On Pombal's orders the Jesuits were confined from May 1759 and shipped to Lisbon in July 1760. Their property was confiscated and sold, including the Quinta Grande.

chapters.title_en: The book and regional dress in its setting
chapters.summary: A short bibliographical note on the 1910 book is followed by a quoted newspaper text. It argues that dress reflects landscape and climate, comparing colourful Madeiran costume with that of the Minho and the plain dress of Porto Santo, and notes variations between municipalities.

The article proposes that the Tourism Delegation commission dolls dressed by local seamstresses for a permanent exhibition. It also urges the preservation of home weaving and vegetable dyeing, and suggests costume contests at the year-end festivities in Funchal.

chapters.title_en: Limits and creation of the parish
chapters.summary: Santo António borders several parishes and was carved out of the Sé parish. It probably began as a curacy in 1557 and became a full parish around 1566.
Royal decrees from 1574 onward raised the priests' stipends; a second curacy was created in 1602. Stipends were abolished in 1911.
The parish began in a chapel of Santo António; a larger church was built in the early seventeenth century and badly damaged by the 1748 earthquake.
The new church was built 1783–1789 on chestnut-trunk foundations, with later works on towers and chapels, including the Guadalupe chapel.
Lists the chapels, the Quinta do Trapiche, the localities, schools and population, road works, publications, 1922–28 improvements and a proposed split of the parish.

abstract: Surveys the history of sugar production in Madeira, from its fifteenth- and sixteenth-century boom and later decline against Brazilian and American competition, to its revival after the vine disease of the nineteenth century and the protected regime of the 1930s. chapters.title_en: Early sugar industry and its taxes
chapters.summary: Madeiran sugar was famous in Europe in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and was pressed in hand presses and mills. The lord of the island took a share of production, trade rules for foreigners and exports were eased, and output rose to over 300,000 arrobas by the mid-sixteenth century.

Competition from Brazil and Spanish America ruined the industry, and Madeira imported sugar from 1736. Cane growing returned after oidium destroyed the vineyards, and production rose sharply up to 1916.
Sugar prices are set according to the price of cane. Decrees of 1928 and 1934 left the Torreão factory as the only sugar maker and limited production to local consumption.

abstract: Biography of Manuel Tomás (1585–1665), a poet born in Guimarães who settled in Funchal, probably as a canon of the cathedral, and wrote the epic poem A Insulana on the discovery and history of Madeira. chapters.summary: Manuel Tomás was born in Guimarães in 1585, settled in Funchal and was probably a canon of the cathedral. He was murdered in 1665, and the Elucidário rejects Azevedo's claim that the killing was linked to the sedition of 1668.

His epic A Insulana, published in Flanders in 1635, tells the history of Madeira and was widely read on the island. Inocêncio praises its merits despite its Gongorist excesses. He also wrote the Phenix da Lusitânia.

abstract: Account of slavery in Madeira from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century: the origins and numbers of slaves, their role in land clearance and the sugar industry, the laws governing them, and their gradual abolition after 1761–1773.

chapters.summary: Black Africans, captive Moors and Canary Islanders cleared Madeira's land in the early colonial period. By 1552 there were about 3,000 slaves in Funchal, and some even came from India.

Slaves drove the sugar boom and, by improving the land, helped create the colonia tenancy contract. They were said to be treated more humanely than in other colonies, though harsh punishments were still allowed.

Royal decrees of 1761, 1768 and 1773 gradually ended slavery in Madeira. Black and Moorish communities formed in Funchal, Ponta do Sol, Machico and Curral das Freiras and mixed with the rest of the population. Earlier laws had restricted runaway and independent slaves.

chapters.summary: The entry recalls the earlier article on patron saints and explains that it reproduces the authentic text of the records published by Funchal city council.

The municipal record tells how plague ravaged Funchal from 1521 to 1538 despite quarantine, until the councillors abolished the guards in 1538 and entrusted the city to St James, after which the plague ceased.
The 1523 record describes the drawing of lots in 1521 that chose St James the Less, the founding of his chapel, and the perpetual vow of an annual procession on 1 May.
The first chapel was a modest hermitage; a new chapel was blessed in 1632, and the present church, begun in 1754, received the saint's image in 1789.

abstract: The boarfish (Capros aper), an uncommon fish in Madeiran waters, caught with hook and line.

Entry on the parish of Caniço, in the municipality of Santa Cruz, Madeira. It covers the origin of its name, its position on the boundary between the captaincies of Funchal and Machico, its early settlers and entailed estates, its churches and clergy, its local products and industries, its levadas and its principal localities.

chapters.summary: The parish takes its name from the reed that grew there. It lay on the boundary between the two captaincies and was settled early by noble families, who founded entailed estates. Two churches were built, one on each bank of the stream.

Although there were two churches, there was only ever one parish and one vicar. The entry records the stipends granted by royal decrees, the parish priests up to the eighteenth century, and the offices of treasurer, curate and organist.

The old churches fell into ruin, and a new parish church was built between 1779 and 1783 on land given by Father José Lomelino Barreto. The entry also lists the parish chapels and quotes Frutuoso's description of the village. Camacha was separated from Caniço in 1676.

The parish had close links with the Desertas and was the birthplace of notable people. The first mill in Madeira is said to have been built here. Onion growing and palm-leaf hats were local specialities, and the entry closes with the parish's schools, levadas, localities, boundaries and population.

abstract: Suburban parish of Funchal, separated from São Pedro and created under a royal charter of 1579, named after its original chapel of São Roque. The entry traces the history of its parish church and lists its chapels, principal localities and population.

chapters.summary: The parish lands first belonged to the Sé parish and later to São Pedro. São Roque was created in 1579 by royal charter, and the priest's stipend was raised in 1589.

The parish took its name from the chapel of São Roque. That church was enlarged in 1704 and collapsed around 1790, and the present church was built slowly during the nineteenth century. The entry ends with the parish's chapels, its localities and its population in 1921.

abstract: Biography of D. Matilde Isabel de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt, Viscondessa das Nogueiras (1805–1888), a Madeiran poet, novelist and translator. She wrote the novel Soldado de Aljubarrota and translated Herculano's Eurico o Presbítero into French.

chapters.summary: Born in Funchal in 1805 to a distinguished family, she wrote verse and prose. Her works include a novel, a school textbook and translations from French.

She translated Eurico o Presbítero into French, published in Paris in 1888, and kept working into old age. She suffered through the 1868 riot against her son and the death of her husband, was praised by Bulhão Pato, and died in 1888.

abstract: Reproduces the 1896 chemical and bacteriological analysis by Charles Lepierre of the cold spring water of São Roque at Machico, long reputed for its therapeutic virtues. The water was classed as hypothermal, hyposaline and sodium-chloride, and found free of coliform bacteria.

chapters.summary: The Elucidário introduces the São Roque spring at Machico and reproduces Lepierre's report. The chemical analysis lists the salts dissolved in the water and confirms that the results are accurate.

abstract: First part of the entry on livestock in Madeira, describing the origins, breeds and uses of cattle, horses, mules, donkeys, sheep, goats and pigs, with nineteenth-century census figures, price rises and the damage caused by free grazing in the mountain forests. It closes by citing sources and introducing a 1941 newspaper editorial on improving cattle breeding.

chapters.summary: Madeiran cattle probably descend from Minho and Algarve stock; English and other breeds introduced from 1802 produced the crossbred 'English cattle'. Porto Santo oxen are small but prized for work, and crossbreeding increased milk yield at the expense of strength.

chapters.title_pt: Gado cavalar, muar, ovino e caprino
chapters.summary: Horse breeding is minor and confined to the upland plateaux. Sheep and goats roam the mountains despite the 1913 grazing law, and angry herders were blamed for the forest fires of August 1919; goat skins, milk and kid meat are used.

Local and imported pig breeds are described, pigs being vital to peasants for manure and meat. Census figures for 1851, 1873 and 1893 are given, together with sharp price rises driven by demand for milk for butter-making.

The author urges better pasture instead of burning forests, recommends João Tierno's report and Alberto Artur Sarmento's book, and begins quoting a 1941 Diário de Notícias editorial on rational cattle breeding.

chapters.title_pt: Selecção do gado e orientação pecuária
chapters.summary: The author argues that Madeiran farmers breed cattle without method, neglect animal health and raise almost no beef cattle. He proposes high-yield dairy cows in the suburban parishes and cream-rich cows for cheese and butter further away. He calls for payment according to meat quality and a stable policy from the Junta Geral.

This closing part of the entry on livestock criticises the lack of breed selection and animal husbandry in Madeira and proposes dairy breeds near Funchal and cream-rich breeds for cheese and butter in outlying parishes. abstract: History of the João Diniz springs beside the São Lourenço fortress in Funchal, a long-used public water source for townspeople and ships, which disappeared in November 1939 during repairs to the palace.

chapters.summary: The springs first appear in a fortification regulation issued soon after the French corsair sack of 1566. Their name probably comes from an early owner, and Frutuoso already used it in 1590; Dr Barral praised the water.

abstract: Biography of Padre Dr João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo, Madeiran priest, vicar of Santa Cruz, lawyer and polemical journalist who edited Madeira's second newspaper, the Pregador Imparcial (1823). A liberal, he was publicly flogged at the Funchal pillory in 1822 and was deported for political crimes in 1823.

chapters.summary: Macedo was a theology graduate who served as chaplain and then vicar of Santa Cruz, and was imprisoned in 1811. He edited the Pregador Imparcial in 1823 and wrote a violent anonymous pamphlet printed in London in 1825. He was elected substitute deputy in 1822.

In February 1822 artillery officers dragged him from his home and flogged him at the pillory. He was known both as a public insulter and as a notable orator and journalist. He was deported to Gibraltar in 1823 and died in 1828.

abstract: Biography of António Aurélio da Costa Ferreira (1879–1922), Funchal-born anthropologist, teacher, director of the Casa Pia and minister of finance, regarded as Portugal's leading physical anthropologist of his day. He died by suicide in Lourenço Marques in 1922, and a Funchal street was renamed after him.

chapters.summary: Costa Ferreira was born in Funchal in 1879, studied at Coimbra and held teaching and academic posts in Lisbon. He served as finance minister and published important anthropological studies of the Portuguese people.

After visiting Funchal in June 1922 he went to Lourenço Marques to organise an anthropological museum, but took his own life there in July 1922. His widow received a pension and Funchal renamed the Rua do Carmo after him.

abstract: Account of the sack of Funchal in October 1566 by French corsairs, many of them Huguenots, under Bertrand de Montluc, instigated by the renegade Portuguese trader Gaspar Caldeira, and of its diplomatic aftermath. It closes with an article by Stephen Gaselee on a letter from Cardinal Henrique relating to the affair.

chapters.summary: Gaspar Caldeira, exiled in France, plotted revenge on Madeira with Bertrand de Montluc. A fleet of about 1,200 men left Bordeaux in September 1566, attacking Porto Santo first.

The corsairs landed at Praia Formosa on 3 October, took the São Lourenço fortress, where Montluc was killed, and plundered Funchal for sixteen days, killing about 300 people. Protests to Charles IX led only to Caldeira's execution.
A 1937 article by Stephen Gaselee transcribes a letter from Cardinal Henrique of December 1566 to the French ambassador and discusses whether Forquevaux was ambassador in Lisbon or Madrid.

abstract: Describes Funchal Bay, the largest harbour of the Madeira archipelago, its limits, shelter, tides and distances to other ports, with statistics of its shipping and trade in the 1930s and 1940s. It shows Funchal as the leading port of the Adjacent Islands and fourth in Portugal.

abstract: History of provision for the mentally ill in Madeira, from a 1493 request for a 'Tronco' to the founding of the Manicómio Câmara Pestana at the Quinta do Rochedo (1906) and the Casa de Saúde de São João de Deus at the Trapiche (1922–24).

chapters.title_en: Early care of the insane and the campaign for an asylum
chapters.summary: Early records show little provision for the mentally ill, who were held in poor conditions in the hospital or in police cells. Growing numbers, partly blamed on alcoholism, led to a press campaign and a founding committee.

chapters.title_en: Founding of the Manicómio Câmara Pestana
chapters.summary: After Câmara Pestana's death in 1899 a committee raised funds, bought the Quinta do Rochedo in 1904 and opened the asylum in 1906, later handing it to the Junta Geral. In 1924 male patients were moved to the Trapiche.

chapters.title_en: The Casa de Saúde do Trapiche
chapters.title_pt: Casa de Saúde de São João de Deus
chapters.summary: The Brothers of Saint John of God, backed by the bishops, occupied the Quinta do Trapiche in 1922, admitted mental patients from 1923 and received the men from the Rochedo in 1924.

chapters.title_en: Pilgrimages, improvements and early years at Trapiche
chapters.summary: Processions from many parishes brought gifts to the new asylum, and the brothers built a road, telephone link and water supply. Patient numbers rose from 2 in 1923 to 104 in 1928, and chaplains served both the house and the parish.

New pavilions, a chapel, staff housing and a dairy were built, and patients worked in workshops and gardens. Doctors applied modern methods such as electroshock, the order gained legal status in 1940, and a new church opened in 1936.

chapters.title_en: The Câmara Pestana asylum for women
chapters.summary: From 1924 the Câmara Pestana asylum took only women, and from 1925 it was run by the Hospitaller Sisters of the Sacred Heart. Its patients grew from 64 in 1926 to 286 in 1943.

abstract: Account of the special judicial tribunal (alçada) sent to Madeira in 1823, after the restoration of absolutism, to investigate and punish supporters of the constitutional government; it sentenced 24 people, mostly from the island's leading classes.

chapters.summary: After absolutism was restored in 1823, the new governor arrived in Madeira with troops and six magistrates. A storm delayed the judges' landing, and they set up their court in the town hall from August to November 1823.
The inquiry spread fear and heard many witnesses. On 26 October it condemned 24 people to exile and other penalties, including notable Madeiran writers, clergy and officials.

abstract: The Recolhimento das Órfãs (also called the Orfanato or Recolhimento de Santa Isabel) was a charitable home in Funchal for orphan girls and women. It was founded in 1725 by Governor Francisco da Costa Freire and was later maintained by the Misericórdia. The entry traces its rules, its residents and its costs up to 1921.

chapters.summary: The home was founded in 1725 with alms and at first took in four orphans. It was run under the Compromisso de Lisboa. A regimento of 1849 was never put into effect, and José Silvestre Ribeiro's plan to turn it into a casa pia failed.
The home stood next to the old Hospital, and the Misericórdia paid the residents' subsidies. The entry gives the numbers of residents and staff and their pay for 1909–1921.

abstract: Biography of D. Luís de Figueiredo de Lemos (1544–1608), Azorean-born seventh bishop of Funchal, remembered as a vigorous reformer of the diocese who built the old episcopal palace and founded the diocesan seminary there.

chapters.summary: Born on Santa Maria in the Azores in 1544, he studied canon and civil law at Coimbra and held church offices in São Miguel and Angra. He was appointed bishop of Funchal in 1585 and arrived in Madeira in 1586.

He reformed parish administration through pastoral visits, built the episcopal palace and São Luís chapel, founded the seminary, held a synod in 1587 and restored São Pedro parish. He died in 1608; his remains were moved to the cathedral in 1903.

abstract: Survey of Madeira's coastline features: the two bays (Funchal and Porto Santo), the small coves, the landing places graded as good, fair or poor, and the island's mostly pebble beaches. It serves as an index pointing to the individual entries on each port and beach.

chapters.summary: Only Funchal and Porto Santo are counted as bays, and a list of small coves follows. The ports are graded as good, fair or poor, and the entry notes that small quays built over the previous thirty years have improved many of them.

Madeira's beaches are short and made of dark basalt pebbles, except for Prainha. Porto Santo, by contrast, has one of the finest sandy beaches in Portugal. The main beaches of the south and north coasts are then listed.

abstract: Biography of Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, son of João Gonçalves Zarco and reputedly the first of his children born in Madeira, who fought in North Africa, leased the Lombada da Ponta do Sol and bought the captaincy of São Miguel in the Azores. He governed that captaincy from 1474 until his death shortly after 1497.

chapters.summary: Rui Gonçalves was Zarco's second son and probably the first born in Madeira. He fought bravely in Africa at Arzila and Tangier, and in 1473 leased his great estate, the Lombada da Ponta do Sol, to João Esmeraldo.

He bought the captaincy of São Miguel from João Soares de Albergaria and settled there in 1474. He granted land in sesmaria, made his will in 1497 and was buried at Vila Franca; his natural son founded the lines of the counts of Vila Franca and Ribeira Grande.

After Henry's death in 1460 the islands passed to Prince Fernando, then to his sons João and Diogo, and finally to D. Manuel, who brought the Order's mastership to the Crown.
D. Manuel's charter of 1497 declared Madeira forever inalienable from the Crown. A later sham grant by D. João IV to his daughter Catarina never took effect.
