abstract: Biography of João Gonçalves da Câmara (c.1414–1501), son of Zarco and second captain-donatary of Funchal, who fought in North Africa, repelled a Castilian attack on Madeira and Porto Santo, and founded the Convent of Santa Clara.

abstract: History of the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau, one of Funchal's earliest churches, begun around 1438 on the shore by the Ribeira de João Gomes, repeatedly damaged by floods and finally destroyed by the great flood of 1803. Its ruins were demolished in 1835 to make way for a fruit and vegetable market.

chapters.summary: The church had several names: Conceição de Baixo, Santa Maria Maior and Nossa Senhora do Calhau, the last after the pebble beach nearby. It was begun around 1438, damaged by the 1611 flood and rebuilt between 1664 and 1688.

Floods in 1707 and 1803 wrecked the church, and its ruins were demolished in 1835 for the Mercado União. The parish moved to the church of Santiago, and the text discusses Funchal's first church, the site and the adjoining hospital.

abstract: Article on the 17th-century Portuguese writer, soldier and diplomat D. Francisco Manuel de Melo, a descendant of Zarco's line, who popularised the Machim legend of Madeira's discovery in his third Epanaphora and stopped in Madeira in 1655 on his way to exile in Brazil. It also discusses Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo's theory that Madeira was secretly considered for cession to England as part of D. Catarina's dowry.

chapters.summary: Melo descended from the Câmara family through Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco's son. An anecdote about his ancestor Antão Rodrigues da Câmara is quoted, and Azevedo notes Melo's inexact claim of direct male descent.

chapters.title_en: Stay in Madeira and the Machim story
chapters.title_pt: Estada na Madeira e a Epanáfora
chapters.summary: In 1655 the fleet taking Melo to exile in Brazil stayed almost a month in Madeira. His third Epanaphora is judged a romantic fiction about Machim, and the 1671 Relation is called a fraud for which he bore no blame.

Azevedo argued that Queen Luísa de Gusmão was ready to cede Madeira to England and that Melo wrote his narrative to help. Edgar Prestage rejects Melo's involvement, and the question remains unresolved.

abstract: History of sugar cane in Madeira from its introduction around 1425, through the sugar boom of the 16th century, its decline, the 19th-century revival after the vine diseases and the cane disease of 1882–86, to cane varieties, prices, cultivation and 20th-century sugar legislation.

chapters.summary: Sugar cane arrived around 1425, spread from Funchal to Machico and to other Atlantic colonies, and peaked in the mid-16th century. Competition from Brazilian sugar ruined the industry, which had largely ended by 1748.

After the vineyards were destroyed in 1846–52, brandy distilleries and sugar mills multiplied across the island. A fungal disease wrecked the canefields from 1882, but new varieties restored them by 1890.
Describes the cane varieties grown, their sugar content and altitude limits, and the changing legal prices paid for cane from 1862 to 1937.
Covers the area under cane, planting, irrigation by levadas, the number of mills, the Hinton factory's dominance, and the 1934 decree regulating the sugar regime.

chapters.title_en: Background and foundation of the diocese
chapters.summary: Funchal was the first diocese created in Portugal's overseas possessions and later became an archbishopric. King Manuel obtained its creation from Pope Leo X in 1514, removing Madeira from the Order of Christ's church jurisdiction. The first bishop, D. Diogo Pinheiro, never came, and only the fourth, D. Jorge de Lemos, took office in person.

The bull Pro excellenti praeeminentia founded the see; it was printed in the Corpo Diplomatico Portuguez and translated in 1897. A companion bull informed the king, and an original parchment once hung in the old episcopal palace.

abstract: Describes the estufas, heated stores used since 1794 to age Madeira wine artificially, their methods and improved systems, and the controversy over their use.

chapters.summary: Estufas began on Madeira in 1794, were banned briefly and then permitted again in 1804. Traditional hot-air and sun estufas heat new wine for months to make it seem older, often giving it a toasted taste.

Improved heating methods, including the Conde do Canavial's establishment of 1889 and steam-coil tanks, reduced the cooked taste. Estufas were blamed for discrediting Madeira wine in 1834, but they were also defended as useful to honest merchants.

abstract: The islet at the western end of Funchal harbour, known simply as 'the Ilhéu', site of the Nossa Senhora da Conceição fortress, a harbour light and a signal station, and joined to the shore in 1890 by the Pontinha breakwater. chapters.title_en: The islet and its early history

abstract: Account of the sugar-cane mills (engenhos) of Madeira from the first mill of 1452 to the 51 factories of the early twentieth century, covering the decline of the sugar industry, the Hinton monopoly and early production methods.

chapters.summary: Madeira had 51 cane-crushing factories, only two able to make sugar on a large scale. Under the sugar regime of 1904 and 1911, 49 distilled only aguardente.

The first mill dates from 1452; the industry declined against American sugar and nearly vanished by the eighteenth century, reviving in the nineteenth. W. Hinton came to dominate sugar and alcohol production by law.

The Torreão factory was the island's leading industrial plant; others included José Julio de Lemos, S. João and Ponte Nova. Early mills were water- or ox-driven, and sugar refining passed from Madeira to Lisbon.

abstract: Biography of Gaspar Frutuoso (1522–1591), Azorean priest and humanist, author of the Saudades da Terra, a key early source for the history of the Atlantic islands including Madeira. It also covers the 1922 centenary edition of his work and the 1866 transfer of his remains.

chapters.summary: Frutuoso was born in Ponta Delgada in 1522, studied theology at Salamanca and refused bishoprics. He served as vicar of Ribeira Grande, where he wrote the Saudades da Terra and died in 1591.

For the 1922 centenary a Ponta Delgada commission published books three and four of the Saudades, with studies by João Simas and Rodrigo Rodrigues. His remains were moved to the municipal cemetery in 1866.

abstract: Biography of D. José de Sousa Castelo Branco, a native of Leiria who was the 14th bishop of Funchal (appointed 1697, resident 1698–1717). He was noted for his pastoral zeal and for defending church privileges against the governor and the royal treasury official.

chapters.summary: Born in Leiria to noble parents, he was appointed bishop of Funchal in 1697 and consecrated in Lisbon in 1698. He ministered at Mazagão before arriving in Funchal on 29 August 1698.

He governed the diocese strictly for 19 years and won a royal inquiry into his conflict with the governor and the treasury official. He left for Portugal in 1717, resigned four years later and died in 1746.

abstract: Describes the Whitsun (Holy Spirit) festivities in Madeiran parishes, with their decorated impérios, parish collecting committees, meals and clothing for the poor, and the former crowning of an 'emperor'. chapters.summary: Parish committees in red capes collect alms with music and sung hymns to pay for the impérios. Twelve poor people receive a meal and a suit of clothes. The crowned 'emperor' disappeared about forty years earlier.

A passage from José de Torres traces the institution to the German emperor Otto, who founded it as a relief fund for times of famine. In the 18th century impérios were held in every street of Funchal, often with excess, but they now take place only near the parish churches.

abstract: Short history of the Archdiocese of Funchal, created in 1533 as the metropolitan see for Portugal's overseas dioceses (Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa) and abolished in 1551. Its only archbishop was D. Martinho de Portugal.

abstract: Entry on the small parish of Achadas da Cruz in the far north-west of Madeira, in the municipality of Porto Moniz, covering its boundaries, localities, ecclesiastical history from a sixteenth-century chapel to independent parish status in 1848, and notable figures and events such as the benefactor Manuel de Pontes Câmara and the 1909 wreck of the yacht Varuna.

abstract: Biography of D. Patrício Xavier de Moura, a friar from Setúbal who became bishop of Cabo Verde, reputedly after winning a wager at backgammon, and later bishop of Funchal (1859–1872). His Funchal episcopate was troubled by conflicts with the cathedral chapter and local politicians.

chapters.title_en: The backgammon promise and Cabo Verde
chapters.title_pt: O codilho e o bispado de Cabo Verde
chapters.summary: An anecdote tells how Viscount Vila Nova de Ourém promised to make the prior of Vila Franca a bishop and did so on becoming a minister. As bishop of Cabo Verde for about ten years, Moura was strict and zealous, quarrelled with the governor-general and gave money to the hungry during a famine.

Transferred to Funchal in 1859, he faced hostility from the chapter and local politicians, and a hostile pamphlet attacked his rule. He obtained Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos as coadjutor and died in Lisbon in 1872.

abstract: Describes Caniçal, the isolated fishing parish at the eastern tip of Madeira, covering its origins as a Moniz entail and hunting reserve, its creation as a parish around 1561, its churches and sea procession, and its landscape, bays and peaks.

chapters.summary: Caniçal is a poor, isolated fishing village cut off from Machico by cliffs. It grew from an estate of Vasco Martins Moniz, entailed to his son Garcia Moniz, and was also the hunting reserve of João Teixeira.

The parish was created about 1561 with an unusually generous stipend. Its church, damaged by the 1748 earthquake, was rebuilt in 1749–50, and a sea procession goes yearly to the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade.
The land is dry and largely uncultivated; an old levada once brought water. The entry notes the fossils, São Lourenço point, Abra bay, the sandy Prainha, the peaks and the main localities.

abstract: Discusses the successive residences of João Gonçalves Zargo in Funchal: a wooden house by the Santa Catarina chapel, a stone house near São Paulo, and his final home near the Conceição de Cima (Santa Clara) church, identified by the author with the present Quinta das Cruzes. abstract: Biography of D. Frei João do Nascimento, Franciscan bishop of Funchal from 1741 to 1753 and governor of Madeira from 1747 to 1751. He built the Episcopal Palace, promoted the building of the Monte church and dealt with the aftermath of the 1748 earthquake.

chapters.summary: He was born in Lisbon to a noble family and took a doctorate in canon law at Coimbra. He then became a Franciscan at Varatojo and was named bishop of Funchal in 1740, against his own wishes.

He was an austere bishop who also governed the archipelago from 1747 to 1751. He built the Episcopal Palace, backed the building of the Monte church and obtained funds for repairs after the 1748 earthquake. He died in 1753 and was buried in the Cathedral.

abstract: Pico Ruivo is the highest peak of Madeira, lying at the southern edge of Santana parish; the entry describes the routes to its summit, the historical measurements of its height (1,861 m according to the 1914 geodetic survey), its panorama, vegetation and geology, and the shelter built there in 1939.

chapters.summary: The peak lies mainly in Santana parish, with spurs in Faial and São Jorge. It can be climbed from Santana or, preferably, from Curral das Freiras, and it offers a view of the island's mountain system.
A table lists height measurements from 1811 to 1914. The 1914 figure of 1,861 m by Colonel Alfredo Durão's geodetic commission is considered the most accurate.

The summit views, the sunrise, the plants and volcanic rocks are described. The entry also covers the division of the peak between parishes, the Lapa da Cadela cave, the 1939 shelter and writings about excursions.

abstract: Biography of Luiz da Câmara Pestana (1863–1899), the Funchal-born bacteriologist who founded and directed the Bacteriological Institute of Lisbon and died of plague contracted while studying the Porto epidemic. It also records the honours paid to his memory in Lisbon and Funchal.

chapters.title_en: Birth, studies and mission to Paris
chapters.title_pt: Nascimento, estudos e missão a Paris
chapters.summary: Câmara Pestana was born in Funchal in 1863, studied medicine in Lisbon and was sent to Paris in 1891 to study bacteriology and Koch's tuberculin. There he worked in leading laboratories and presented research on tetanus toxins.

Back in Lisbon he became bacteriology demonstrator, showed a new treatment for tetanus and, after being asked to analyse Lisbon's water, founded the Bacteriological Institute in 1892. His many publications are listed.

He became a professor and hospital surgeon, then died in 1899 of plague caught in Porto. The king, Lisbon and Funchal honoured him with a pension, the institute's name, an asylum, a street and a memorial plaque.

abstract: First part of a history of political parties in Madeira, from the liberal–absolutist divide of the early nineteenth century through the Cartist, Septembrist, Regenerator, Progressive, Fusionist, Popular and Franquist groupings, up to the early divisions among republicans in 1911. It names the leading local politicians of each faction, their newspapers, and the electoral violence that marked island politics.

chapters.summary: Liberals and absolutists, later constitutionalists and Miguelists, gave way after 1834 to Cartists and Septembrists. The despotism of Costa Cabral first stirred bitter political passions in Madeira, leading to the Junta Governativa of 1847 and violent elections.

chapters.title_en: Regeneration, Fusion and the Popular party
chapters.summary: Madeiran politicians split between Regenerators and Historical Progressives, which later merged into the Fusionist party. The struggle between Fusionists and the Popular party in 1868–70 brought riots, killings and bombings to the island.

chapters.title_en: Progressives, Regenerator split and the Republic
chapters.summary: The modern Progressive party was organised in 1876 and the Regenerators split in 1901, followed by fierce electoral fighting. Franquist and Nationalist groups also appeared, and after the Republic of 1910 the monarchist parties vanished while republicans soon divided.

Madeiran republicans divided into Democrats, Evolutionists and Unionists after 1911. Most Democrats later joined Álvaro de Castro's Reconstituição Nacional in 1920. Monarchists dominated the island under Sidónio Pais.

Small parties such as the Catholic, Labour, Integralist and Radical parties appeared in Madeira, and the Reconstituintes joined the Nationalist party in 1923. The author ends by admitting that his account is incomplete and points readers to the local newspapers.

abstract: Biography of João António Monteiro (1769–1834), a Funchal-born mineralogist and Coimbra professor who left Portugal in 1804 on a scientific journey and won a European reputation for his work in crystallography and mineralogy.

abstract: First part of the entry on Madeira's forest regime: it recalls the dense primeval forest found by the first settlers, its destruction by fire, felling and timber export, and the royal regulations of 1493, 1515 and 1562 and later laws meant to protect it. It also denounces grazing, charcoal-making and the timber trade as the chief enemies of the woods.

chapters.summary: Early chroniclers and navigators described the island as entirely covered by tall, dense forest of many valuable species. This abundance explains the island's name.

chapters.title_pt: O incêndio e a exportação das madeiras
chapters.summary: Settlers cleared land by a great fire and then exploited timber for houses, ships and export, using water-powered sawmills. Madeiran timber even changed building styles in Portugal.
Royal charters of 1493, 1515 and 1562 restricted felling, required tree planting and punished offenders. Later decrees and a nursery at Monte continued conservation efforts.
Shepherds, charcoal-burners and timber merchants are blamed for destroying the woods, often by fire. The grazing laws of 1913 and 1917 are judged ineffective.
The 1562 regiment introduced municipal licences for cutting timber. The author argues that these licences have long been used as cover for the large-scale felling of Madeira's forests.

In 1928 the Junta Geral asked the central government for a forestry expert. The forestry engineer José Augusto Fragoso delivered a report in 1929 that proposed a Forestry District, reafforestation and a decree on grazing.

In 1945 the number of forest posts and guards was increased. The author traces how forest administration passed from the donataries to the municipal councils and then to later state bodies, and notes the lack of a comprehensive law.

chapters.title_en: The baldios and the case for a Forestry District
chapters.title_pt: Os baldios e a Circunscrição Florestal
chapters.summary: The uncultivated uplands, or baldios, are poorly delimited and are being alienated, which threatens the customary rights of poor farmers. The author condemns the lax licensing of rare native trees and again calls for a Forestry District.

part_abstracts: First part of the entry on Madeira's forest regime: it recalls the dense primeval forest found by the first settlers, its destruction by fire, felling and timber export, and the royal regulations of 1493, 1515 and 1562 and later laws meant to protect it. It also denounces grazing, charcoal-making and the timber trade as the chief enemies of the woods.

This second part of the entry on Madeira's forestry regime criticises the abuse of felling licences, summarises José Augusto Fragoso's 1929 report on reorganising forest services, and traces the administrative history of forestry on the island. It closes with a discussion of the baldios (common uplands) and a plea for a technically led Forestry District (Circunscrição Florestal).

abstract: Account of the repeated raids and sackings of the undefended island of Porto Santo by French, Moroccan and Algerian corsairs and pirates between 1566 and 1708, with the islanders taking refuge on the Pico do Castelo.

chapters.summary: Porto Santo had almost no defences, so its people fled to the summit of Pico do Castelo when pirates came. Regular fortifications appeared only in the 18th century.

abstract: Describes the rede, a hammock-like litter slung from a pole and carried by two or more men, used in Madeira to transport people, especially invalids and foreign visitors touring the interior. It notes the bearers' remarkable agility and the high cost of hiring them.

The chapel passed through the Carvalhal Esmeraldo family and was rebuilt in the seventeenth century. Other Santo Amaro chapels stood at Lombada dos Esmeraldos and in Santa Cruz.

abstract: History of the diocesan Seminary of Funchal, founded by royal charter of D. Sebastião in 1566 following the Council of Trent, tracing its many changes of premises up to its return to the Incarnação building in 1933. It highlights the founder Bishop D. Jerónimo Barreto, the reformer Bishop D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto and the teacher Padre Ernesto Schmitz.

chapters.summary: The seminary was created in 1566 under the Council of Trent's decrees and set up by Bishop Jerónimo Barreto. It moved between houses, the Jesuit College (1788) and the Mosteiro Novo house after the British occupation of 1801.

Bishop Manuel Agostinho Barreto built a new seminary in 1909, but the 1911 law suppressed it and the State took the building. The entry describes its endowment, curricula, the 1877 reform, Padre Schmitz's work and the return to the building in 1933.

abstract: Entry on Gaspar Frutuoso's sixteenth-century chronicle 'Saudades da Terra', whose second book is the richest source for the early history of Madeira, and on its editions, notably Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo's annotated 1873 Funchal edition. It also discusses the manuscript tradition, later Azorean editions and the debt to Jerónimo Dias Leite.

chapters.title_pt: A obra e as suas fontes
chapters.summary: Frutuoso's work is the main source for Madeira's history in the 15th and 16th centuries. He wrote it as parish priest in Ribeira Grande, São Miguel, using material sent by canon Jerónimo Dias Leite.

Book II was printed in Funchal in 1873 with Azevedo's notes, from a copy obtained from the Agrela da Câmara family. Ernesto do Canto later found the copy inaccurate and corrected much of it against the autograph.
Damião Peres published Book II in Porto in 1925 without Azevedo's notes, which the author regrets. He also questions the choice of the Ajuda codex instead of Canto's corrected copy.

Ponta Delgada published the remaining books from 1922 to 1939 with studies of Frutuoso. João Franco Machado argued in 1937 that the historical chapters were copied from Dias Leite, and the entry lists all published volumes.

abstract: Biography of Francisco Alvares de Nobrega (1772–1806), Machico-born poet nicknamed 'Camões Pequeno', persecuted by Bishop José da Costa Torres and the Inquisition, who took his own life in Lisbon. He is remembered chiefly for his sonnets, published as the Rimas in 1804.

chapters.summary: Nobrega was born in Machico in 1772 and was educated in the house of the merchant Marcos João de Ornelas. At the seminary he wrote satirical verse against Bishop Torres. He was caught up in the bishop's persecution of freemasons, imprisoned and sent to Lisbon.

Bishop Vilares had him freed from the Limoeiro prison, but he was later jailed again by the Inquisition. Ill and despairing, he poisoned himself at the age of 34. His Rimas were published in 1804, and his remaining papers were destroyed after his death.

abstract: Biography of Dr Lourenço José Moniz (1789–1857), Madeiran physician, teacher and long-serving deputy for Madeira, remembered for his integrity and selfless defence of the archipelago's interests.

chapters.summary: Moniz is praised for his talent and austerity. Born in Funchal in 1789 and educated by his uncle, he studied medicine at Edinburgh and returned to practise and teach, becoming the first rector of the Funchal lyceum.

Elected deputy in 1826, he went into exile in the United States under absolutism, then represented Madeira almost continuously from 1834 to 1856. He also served as commissioner for maritime prizes at the Cape of Good Hope.
He was civil governor of Coimbra and a member of the Overseas Council, and died poor in Lisbon in 1857. Madeirans raised a mausoleum for him in the Alto de São João cemetery, whose epitaph is quoted.

abstract: Reviews the competing theories on the origin of the place-name Machico, from the discredited Machim legend to derivations from Monchique, 'macho' and Italian 'macchia', ending with Brito Rebelo's 1894 discovery of a fourteenth-century mariner named Machico. The question mattered because the Machim etymology was used to claim an English precedence in discovering Madeira.

chapters.summary: The origin of the name is still unresolved. Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo argued it mattered because Richard Henry Major used the Machim legend to claim an English discovery of Madeira.

chapters.title_pt: Hipóteses de Azevedo, Bettencourt e Camilo
chapters.summary: Azevedo derived the name from Monchique in the Algarve, which Pinheiro Chagas rejected. Bettencourt suggested a diminutive of 'macho', and Camilo Castelo Branco proposed the Italian 'macchia'.

In 1894 General Brito Rebelo published a royal grant of houses in Lisbon to a mariner called Machico. The Elucidário finds his conclusions overstated but the document valuable against the Machim legend.

abstract: Parish in the municipality of Calheta, Madeira, created in 1572 around the chapel of São Braz; the entry covers its early settlers and sugar estates, its church, chapels and entailed estates, local unrest in 1834 and 1887, and its geography.

chapters.title_en: Origins and the chapel of São Braz
chapters.title_pt: Origem e capela de São Braz
chapters.summary: The name comes from the arc-shaped hills. The parish was created in 1572 at the chapel of São Braz, whose founder is disputed. The chapel was enlarged, and a new church was built between 1744 and 1754.
Early settlers such as João Fernandes de Andrade and Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara held large sugar estates. The entry lists the parish's chapels and the entailed estates attached to them.
The entry recounts the riots of 1834 and 1887, then describes the schools, levadas, boundaries, localities, patron saint, pilgrimage and population.

abstract: The palanquin was a litter carried on a pole by two men, formerly much used in Madeira for transporting invalids and ladies. By the time of writing it had long disappeared, surviving only for carrying child 'angels' to Lenten processions.

chapters.summary: The palanquin probably derived from Indian and Chinese litters. The American John A. Dix, visiting in 1842, described its shoe-shaped body, its pole and its two bearers, and compared it with the hammock.

The palanquin had long fallen out of use. Around forty years before the time of writing it carried only children dressed as angels to processions, though in the early nineteenth century ladies used it for outings and visits.

abstract: Henrique (Henry) Veitch was a British subject who served for many years as English consul in Madeira and died there in 1857. He is remembered for meeting Napoleon aboard the Northumberland in 1815, for his distinctive buildings, and for protecting Madeirans during the Miguelist occupation and the civil wars.

chapters.summary: Veitch was appointed British consul during the second British occupation (1807–1814) and kept good relations with local people. In 1815 he was the only person to board the Northumberland and speak to Napoleon, sending him fruit, sweets and wine.

He spent much of his fortune on property and original buildings, including a house at Jardim da Serra where his mausoleum stands. In 1828 he helped many Madeirans, including the governor, flee to the frigate Alligator.

As deputy he obtained currency unification, road studies, levada legislation and the Pontinha harbour, among other benefits. He held many public and company posts, was honoured after the 1901 royal visit, wrote for newspapers and died in 1912.

abstract: Entry on the water starwort (Callitriche stagnalis), an aquatic plant sometimes used on Madeira as an aperient.

The Junta Agrícola da Madeira was an agricultural board created by the sugar-regime decree of 11 March 1911 and funded by the tax on aguardente (cane spirit). It was meant to expropriate the spirit distilleries, promote Madeira wine abroad and improve agriculture, but the Elucidário judges it largely a failure until its abolition in 1919.

chapters.title_en: Creation and the fight against alcoholism
chapters.title_pt: Criação da Junta e o alcoolismo
chapters.summary: The Junta was created by the 1911 decree that settled the Hinton question. The author praises the planned expropriation of the aguardente factories as a remedy for alcoholism, which he blames for physical and mental decline, and regrets that it was never carried out.

chapters.title_en: Aims and record of the Junta
chapters.summary: Article 26 of the decree set four aims: expropriating distilleries, promoting wine abroad, founding an agricultural station and regrafting vines. Results were poor apart from the nurseries and pest control, while spending on tourism, land purchases and an unused cold store was criticised.

Regulations from 1912 and 1913 changed the Junta's aims and composition and weakened the expropriation clause. An official inquiry in 1915 cleared its members, and later laws gave it the state levadas. It was abolished in 1919.

abstract: João Leitão, a royal judge (desembargador), was sent by the Spanish government as the first governor-general of Madeira after Philip II became king of Portugal. He arrived in 1582 and served until 1585. The entry also discusses Damião Peres's argument that he was governor only de facto and not by formal appointment.

chapters.summary: Under Spanish rule the powers of the captain-donataries declined, and a governor-general was created. João Leitão came to Madeira in 1582 with wide powers and orders to investigate the political events that followed Philip II's proclamation. He governed until 1585.

Damião Peres argued in 1924 that Leitão was governor only in fact, not by law, and that he arrived in 1582. The Elucidário accepts the corrected date but maintains that Leitão was effectively Madrid's representative.

abstract: Biography of D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto (1835–1911), 26th bishop of Funchal from 1876 to 1911, regarded by the Elucidário as the most illustrious prelate of the diocese. It is chiefly noted for his reform of the diocesan seminary and the building of the new seminary at the Incarnação.

chapters.summary: Born in 1835, he trained in theology at Coimbra and held high office in the diocese of Lamego. He was appointed bishop of Funchal in 1876 and consecrated in Lisboa in 1877. Soon after arriving he clashed with the Funchal council over the burial of a suicide.
He lived modestly at Penha de França for 34 years, devoted to his diocese. He reformed the seminary and had a new seminary building erected at the former Incarnação convent.

abstract: Entry on pine trees in Madeira, tracing the introduction and municipal promotion of stone pine and maritime pine from the late eighteenth century, their cultivation and uses, and the other pine species present in the archipelago.

chapters.summary: Stone pines were the first grown in Madeira, and maritime pines came in the late eighteenth century. The Funchal council repeatedly ordered pine seed between 1807 and 1839. Large-scale planting of maritime pine began under José Silvestre Ribeiro.

Maritime pines are felled at 12–15 years, and thinnings are sold as bean poles and trellis wood. Seed is sown from January to March, often with cereals as shelter. Aleppo and Canary pines also grow in the archipelago, including on Porto Santo.

abstract: History of the postal service in Madeira from the appointment of a deputy postmaster in 1662 through state takeover in 1852 and the joint telegraph-postal reorganisation of 1880, with revenue figures.

chapters.summary: Regular post began around 1662 under a deputy postmaster. A Madeira post office was created in 1798, later run by a contracted 'correio assistente' appointed by tender.

abstract: Part 1 of the entry on Funchal Cathedral, a Gothic-Manueline national monument begun in the 1490s under D. Manuel and consecrated in 1516, covering its construction history, architecture, Mudéjar cedar ceiling, chapels, processional cross and organs, followed by the start of a chronology.

chapters.summary: The cathedral was planned on a grand scale in anticipation of the diocese. D. Manuel granted land in 1485 and revenues from 1488 onwards; work began soon after 1493 and the consecration took place in 1516, with later additions continuing into the 18th and 19th centuries.
Frutuoso's 1590 description, the Gothic nave with its famous cedar and ivory ceiling, later alterations, the Blessed Sacrament chapel, D. Manuel's silver-gilt processional cross, and the organs.
The revisers refer readers to their 1936 booklet and begin a dated chronology of the cathedral from 1485 to about 1521.

A year-by-year list of events at Funchal Cathedral, including its brief archiepiscopal status, the 1566 Huguenot sack, the first synod, bishops' burials, later building works, earthquake damage, the clock and bells, and the 1940 museum.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Faial on Madeira's north coast, one of the first northern areas settled, created as a parish in 1550. It covers the origin of its name, its clergy, its church and pilgrimage of 8 September, its bridges and quay, and its localities.

chapters.summary: The parish takes its name from the faia tree. Lançarote Teixeira was an early settler, and the parish was created in 1550 with Padre João Soares as its first vicar.
Floods destroyed the old chapel, so a new church was begun in 1745. Frutuoso's 1590 account describes a great pilgrimage and fair, which still took place in the author's time.
Bridges begun in 1904 and the Viscount of Cacongo quay (1903–05) are described. The entry then lists the parish's boundaries and localities, and its notable natives.

abstract: Biography of António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia (1797–1861), 1st Viscount of Atouguia, a Funchal-born mathematician, liberal soldier in the civil war and politician who served as deputy for Madeira and several times as minister of the navy and of foreign affairs.

chapters.summary: Born in Funchal in 1797 to a noble Madeiran family, he was educated at Old Hall Green near London and graduated in mathematics at Coimbra. He then taught at the Naval Academy.

A liberal, he joined Governor Travassos Valdez in Madeira in 1828, fled to England, then went to Terceira and took part in the failed 1832 expedition against Madeira. He fought in the civil war and was decorated after the battle of Almoster.

He was deputy for Madeira, minister of the navy and of foreign affairs, civil governor of Porto and president of the Chamber of Deputies. He became a peer in 1853, viscount in 1854, and died in Lisbon in 1861.

abstract: Describes the harbour of Porto do Moniz, reputedly the safest and most sheltered anchorage on Madeira's north coast, used as a refuge when southerly winds close the southern ports. It records hydrographic studies of 1914 and harbour works carried out between 1901 and 1916.

abstract: First part of the entry on the English (British) in Madeira, covering British designs on the archipelago, the consulate, the colony's commercial dominance, especially of the wine trade, its privileges, churches and institutions, and its social influence up to 1921.

chapters.summary: Britain is said to have long wanted Madeira, from Catarina's marriage to the two occupations and an 1897 press campaign. The diplomat Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho secured the island's return to Portugal.

The British colony grew from 1640, with a consulate from 1658, and came to monopolise the wine trade. The British even levied their own export duties, the 'direitos de nação', and offered the governor an annual payment.
The British had their own judge-conservator, registry, Protestant churches, cemetery and a hospital ward. Many came for the climate, and British naturalists studied the islands.

abstract: First part of the entry on Funchal, covering the origin of its name (from the fennel plant, funcho), the creation of the town and municipality around 1451–52, and its elevation to city status by King Manuel I in 1508, with the royal charter transcribed in full.

chapters.summary: Funchal is said to take its name from the fennel that grew abundantly in the valley where the settlers landed. The entry also notes other places called Funchal in mainland Portugal.

chapters.title_en: Creation of the town and municipality
chapters.title_pt: II – Criação da vila e município
chapters.summary: Early settlement grew near the João Gomes stream, and Funchal became a town around 1451, receiving a charter from Afonso V in 1452. Its municipal area was later reduced, reaching its present extent in 1835.

King Manuel I raised Funchal to city status by royal letter of 21 August 1508, the first city of Portugal's overseas domains. A few days earlier he ordered its council to be governed like that of Lisbon.

Madeira was first divided into three captaincies, then became a single administrative district in 1834 under a prefect, later a civil governor. The Funchal municipality's parishes and boundaries are listed.
Funchal is described as an amphitheatre-like city on the south coast, praised for its climate, flowers, wine and hospitality, with quotations from other writers.
The town council fixed the city limits in 1809, 1863 and 1909, and in 1927 greatly enlarged them to include suburban parishes, raising the area from about 500 to about 750 hectares.

abstract: Discusses Plato's legendary Atlantis and later scientific theories of a sunken Atlantic continent, concluding that Madeira and its neighbouring islands are an independent volcanic creation rather than remnants of submerged land.

abstract: Survey of entailed estates (morgadios and vínculos) in Madeira, from their foundation in the 15th and 16th centuries to their abolition by the law of 1863. It names the principal founding families and estates, the Pombaline reforms and the 1849 attempt by the Barão de São Pedro to abolish them locally.

chapters.summary: Madeira had an unusually large number of entailed estates, perhaps two-thirds of its land. Early settlers received land grants, grew rich on sugar, then entailed their land and moved to the towns.
Lists entails founded in the late 15th and early 16th centuries and the wealthy houses that survived. The records of the old Juízo dos Resíduos e Capelas were long thought lost.

Pombal's laws of 1769 and 1770 reduced entails; an 1849 bill to abolish them in Madeira failed, but the 1863 law abolished them nationwide. Further houses are noted from Alfredo Pimenta's book, and surviving records reached the District Archive.

abstract: Biography of João Maria Moniz (1822–1898), Funchal tax official and self-taught naturalist, chiefly a botanist and malacologist, who built important herbaria and shell collections and introduced many exotic plants to Madeira. Several species and the genus Monizia were named after him.

chapters.summary: Moniz was born in Funchal in 1822 and worked in the Funchal revenue office until 1895. He built a herbarium, partly lost with Lowe's shipwreck, and species and the genus Monizia were named after him. He first recorded Visnea mocanera in Madeira.
He acclimatised exotic plants at Desterro, received honours and royal gifts, and left herbarium, shell and wood collections. He died in Funchal in 1898 without publishing any work.

abstract: This first part recounts the Hohenlohe concession of 1903 to build tuberculosis sanatoria in Madeira, the diplomatic dispute that led to its buyback by the Portuguese State in 1909, and reproduces Dr António de Lencastre's 1903 report and a 1914 government notice leasing the confiscated properties at Monte.

chapters.title_en: The Hohenlohe concession and its rescission
chapters.summary: Prince Hohenlohe obtained permission in 1903 to build sanatoria in Madeira and bought several quintas at Monte. A dispute over expropriating the Quinta Pavão, owned by an Englishman, led the government to buy back the concession in 1909 for over 4.7 million marks.
The government's medical delegate describes the German mission's visit, the island's climate, the spread of tuberculosis among the poor, and the planned coastal, mountain and high-altitude sanatoria.
A government notice offers the former company properties, including the Bianchi, Vigia, Reis and Santana quintas and the Arrebentão waters, for lease in a single lot, with its conditions.

part_abstracts: This first part recounts the Hohenlohe concession of 1903 to build tuberculosis sanatoria in Madeira, the diplomatic dispute that led to its buyback by the Portuguese State in 1909, and reproduces Dr António de Lencastre's 1903 report and a 1914 government notice leasing the confiscated properties at Monte.

This closing part explains that, after the failure of the Prince of Hohenlohe's company, the National Assistance for Tuberculosis Patients took on building a sanatorium in Madeira, achieved chiefly through Dr João Francisco de Almada. The sanatorium, built at the former Quinta Santana, opened in 1941 and bears his name.

abstract: Survey of fishing in the Madeira archipelago, chiefly reproducing a 1932 article by the naturalist Adolfo César de Noronha on the sea floor, fishermen's depth zones, the principal fish families, fishing gear and recent changes, followed by notes on the Casas dos Pescadores and catch values in the 1940s.

chapters.summary: The entry introduces Noronha's article and describes Madeira's steep, rugged sea floor. Fishermen divide the deep sea into zones, from the bairil at about 100 fathoms to the alto, altura and altio.
Coastal, pelagic and deep-sea species are reviewed by family, including tuna, black scabbardfish, sea bream, groupers and sharks. Limpets, octopus, squid and turtles are also mentioned.
Hook gear predominates over nets and pots. A tuna trap at Porto Santo (1910–12) failed, while strong lamps improved night fishing, and some boats gained petrol motors.

abstract: Account of Napoleon's passage past Madeira in August 1815 aboard HMS Northumberland on his way to exile on Saint Helena, including the visit of British consul Henry Veitch, and of the 1840 call of the French frigates bringing back his remains.

chapters.title_en: The voyage and the stop at Funchal
chapters.summary: After Waterloo Napoleon was taken aboard the Northumberland towards Saint Helena and the squadron anchored off Funchal on 23–24 August 1815 during a hot leste wind. Consul Henry Veitch visited him and sent fruit and wine; tradition says Napoleon's gold coins were laid in the foundations of the Anglican church.

Extracts from the diary of J. R. Glover, the admiral's secretary, describe Napoleon's gloomy mood, his questions about Madeira and Veitch's visit. Other sources confirm the coins under the Anglican church's first stone.

In July 1840 the French frigates carrying the Prince de Joinville's mission to fetch Napoleon's remains called at Funchal. Consul Monteiro Teixeira gave a ball where General Bertrand offered a lady his ring from Napoleon.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Câmara de Lobos, west of Funchal, covering the origin of its name in the discovery voyage of Zarco, its churches, chapels and collegiate chapter, early settlers, fishing community and renowned vineyards. It also records its localities, boundaries, levadas and population.

Zarco founded the Espírito Santo chapel, first seat of the parish created around 1430; the seat later moved to São Sebastião church. The priests' stipends, the curacy of 1576 and the collegiate chapter are described.
Lists early landholders and entailed estates, the many chapels, the São Bernardino convent, the 1929 landslide disaster and notable natives including Fr. Pedro da Guarda.
Describes the fishing quarter of Ilhéu, the superior wine, iron ore and building stone, then lists localities, boundaries, levadas, population and the road to Funchal.

abstract: Discusses the discovery of Porto Santo, the first island of the archipelago reached by Portuguese navigators, and the traditional explanation of its name as a safe haven from a storm, quoting João de Barros.

abstract: This first part describes the celebrations held in Funchal from 29 December 1922 to 4 January 1923 to mark the fifth centenary of the discovery of Madeira, organised by Major João dos Reis Gomes despite the central government's refusal to take part. It covers the debate on the discovery date, the programme, the committees and the main events, including the Te Deum, the laying of the first stone of the Zarco monument, the exhibitions and the historical procession.

chapters.title_en: The discovery date and the origins of the celebration
chapters.title_pt: Data do descobrimento e iniciativa das festas
chapters.summary: The discovery date was disputed, which allowed the celebration to be postponed until late 1922. Major Reis Gomes launched the idea, helped by the artists Cândido Pereira and Emanuel Ribeiro. The government in Lisbon refused to take part.
This chapter lists the twelve points of the programme drawn up by Reis Gomes. It also gives the committees formed to carry it out and their leading members.

chapters.title_en: The festivities from 29 December to 4 January
chapters.summary: The festivities opened with a Te Deum in the cathedral and a procession to Zarco's tomb, followed by the blessing of the first stone of his monument. There were theatre performances, a fair and agricultural exhibition, and an exhibition of books and art at the Industrial School.

On 4 January a grand procession of allegorical floats passed through the city, representing the nations, Madeira's industries and sport. It was led by a caravel built by master Luís Basílio and closed by the float of Prince Henry.

chapters.title_en: The Infante's car, procession and illuminations
chapters.title_pt: O Carro do Infante e as iluminações
chapters.summary: A press account praises the Infante's allegorical car sculpted by José Pereira, which closed the procession. The entry lists the bodies in the procession, notes the absence of state participation, and describes the fireworks and illuminations from 29 December to 3 January. It concludes that these were the grandest festivities ever held on the island, paid for locally.

part_abstracts: This first part describes the celebrations held in Funchal from 29 December 1922 to 4 January 1923 to mark the fifth centenary of the discovery of Madeira, organised by Major João dos Reis Gomes despite the central government's refusal to take part. It covers the debate on the discovery date, the programme, the committees and the main events, including the Te Deum, the laying of the first stone of the Zarco monument, the exhibitions and the historical procession.

This concluding part describes the allegorical car honouring Infante D. Henrique, the civic procession, fireworks and street illuminations in Funchal at the turn of 1922–1923, and stresses that the quincentenary festivities were funded solely by local resources without government help.

Summary of an article by the naval officer Pires de Matos (1940) on the geodetic triangulations of the Madeira archipelago (1914, 1936) and the astronomical observations used to place its hydrographic charts on the international ellipsoid. It matters as a record of how the islands were first accurately mapped.

chapters.summary: The 1914 triangulation of Madeira was based on the Paul da Serra and had its origin at the Forte de S. Tiago. It was revised in 1936, when Porto Santo and the Desertas were added with a new origin on Porto Santo. The deflection of the vertical made both coordinate systems unsatisfactory.
The Hydrographic Mission observed at seven stations with a German theodolite and applied Hayford's isostatic method. It lists the charts used to calculate the topographic deflections.
Astronomical stations should be placed on level or plateau ground and on the least rugged island. The author defends spending on good instruments for the sake of future science.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Calheta on Madeira's south-west coast, one of the island's oldest settlements, covering the origin of its name, early settlers, church, chapels, clergy, the 1834 riot and its localities.

chapters.title_pt: Origem do nome e primeiros povoadores
chapters.summary: The name comes from the small cove Zarco's men used as a landing place. The discoverer gave land here to his children, and many early settlers received sesmarias and founded chapels.

The parish was created in 1430, first seated at the Estrela chapel and later at the Espírito Santo church, rebuilt in 1639. It had a collegiate chapter, a notable tabernacle given by King Manuel I, many chapels, a Franciscan convent and a Misericórdia.

In July 1834 a riot against the new constitutional order was suppressed by troops, with deaths and later sentences of exile. The entry ends with traces of petroleum, the main localities, schools, distances and population.

Parish on the south-west coast of Madeira, founded on the estate of the legendary Henrique Alemão and made an independent parish in 1582. The entry covers its name, chapels, sugar and banana farming, population, schools, levadas, notable natives and the 1939 flood of the Ribeira da Madalena.

chapters.summary: The parish's location and the origin of its name are described. Its settlement began with the estate and chapel of Henrique Alemão, later rebuilt by João Rodrigues de Freitas, who founded an entailed estate there.

The parish was separated from Ponta do Sol in 1582, and royal charters set the priest's stipend. Gaspar Frutuoso described its sugar mill and chapels, and its fertile soil still produces bananas for export.
The parish had 1,093 inhabitants in 1920, with schools and levadas. Notable natives are named, and the landslide of 1932 and the disastrous flood of 1939 are recorded.

abstract: The captaincy of Porto Santo, one of the three into which the Madeira archipelago was divided, granted to Bartolomeu Perestrelo in 1446 and held by his descendants until the governors replaced the donataries. The entry lists the succession of captains-donatary and explains the island's slow development.

chapters.summary: Porto Santo was granted as a captaincy to Bartolomeu Perestrelo in 1446 with civil and criminal jurisdiction. His descendants held it until Philippine rule reduced the donataries to a largely honorary role.

The succession of Perestrelo donataries is traced, including two who murdered their wives. Governors later replaced them until 1848, and pirate raids, droughts and absentee landowners kept the island poor, prompting the law of 1770.

abstract: History of the Campo da Barca, a public square in Funchal built under Governor Florencio José Correia de Melo and handed to the municipality in 1818, named after the Conde da Barca. The entry also traces its later renamings and the buildings now on the site.

chapters.summary: The square was built by the governor on donated land and handed to the town council in 1818. Its northern part passed to the municipality in 1897.
Official renamings in 1897 and 1911 were ignored by the public. The popular name is a shortening of Campo do Conde da Barca, which honoured the diplomat António de Araújo de Azevedo.
The square lies on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes and is now divided by a street into the Praça de Tenerife and a northern part with health facilities and a monument.

abstract: History of the flag and municipal standard of Funchal from the first banner sent by Infante D. Fernando in the fifteenth century to the flags commissioned under the Republic, based on an article by Carlos Azevedo de Meneses. It also describes who carried the standard in ceremonies.

chapters.title_pt: Da primeira bandeira ao regime constitucional
chapters.summary: Funchal's first flag was sent by Infante D. Fernando; by 1563 it bore St James, and from the 17th century to 1834 it was white with royal and city arms. A costly silk standard was bought from Lisbon in 1815, and after 1834 the colours changed to blue and white.

The National Guard flag was lost, while a blue-and-white monarchy flag survives in the archive. Republican-era flags were made, including those ordered in 1919, and the standard-bearer changed from the procurador to the youngest councillor.

abstract: Sub-entry of 'Clima' describing the prevailing winds of Madeira and Porto Santo from observations made in the early twentieth century, followed by a bibliographical note on climate studies and a long quoted article by Dr Armindo Narciso defending the therapeutic value of the Madeiran climate, especially for tuberculosis patients.

chapters.summary: The north-east wind dominates at Ponta de São Lourenço and Porto Santo. Northerly winds bring snow to the mountains, and westerly winds bring rain. The hot, dry 'leste' wind from Africa is also mentioned.

Hugo de Lacerda's 1936 study of the climate is praised, together with its 1938 English translation. Dr Armindo Narciso describes Madeira's climate as a special oceanic climate with Mediterranean features, gently tonic and soothing.

The British first used Madeira as a health resort, particularly for consumptives. Narciso argues that the later rejection of Madeira for lung patients was a misunderstanding. He holds that carefully selected patients still benefit from the climate.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Ponta do Sol on Madeira's south coast, covering the origin of its name, its settlement from about 1440 by Rodrigo Enes 'o Coxo', its parish church of Nossa Senhora da Luz, its early settlers and entailed estates, notable natives, its quay of 1848 and the royal visit of 1858.

chapters.summary: Gaspar Frutuoso and João Agostinho de Freitas explain the name by a sun-like mark on a rock above a headland near the town.

Rodrigo Enes, the Lame, settled here around 1440–1450 and asked in his will for a chapel in the church. The parish dates from the 15th century, and royal charters fixed the vicar's stipend. The church of Nossa Senhora da Luz was rebuilt in the early 18th century.
Portuguese and foreign settlers received sesmarias here and founded entailed estates. The entry lists distinguished natives and the local historian João Agostinho de Freitas.

abstract: Describes the early prosperity and long decline of Porto Santo, caused by droughts, piracy, absentee landlords and the idleness of would-be nobles, and the Pombaline reform of 1770 known as the 'Law of Fifths and Eighths' that reallocated land to its cultivators.

chapters.summary: Porto Santo prospered briefly after settlement but declined from the late sixteenth century. Droughts, pirates, absent landlords, the colonia contract and residents' pride in noble ancestry left the island near depopulation.

chapters.title_en: The Law of Fifths and Eighths
chapters.summary: The royal charter of 13 October 1770 gave cultivators the useful domain of the land, paying landlords only a fifth or eighth of produce. It also restricted public offices to farmers and ordered idle men's sons to learn trades.

chapters.title_en: Execution of the law and later crises
chapters.summary: Governor Sá Pereira went to Porto Santo in 1771 with officials to apply the law. Twenty years later it was falling into disuse, and droughts continued to bring famine.

abstract: History of the church of São Tiago (now called Socorro) in Funchal, founded in 1523 after a vow to Saint James during plague and famine, rebuilt between 1752 and 1768, and made the seat of the parish of Santa Maria Maior after the 1803 flood.

chapters.summary: The church was built after Funchal's vow to Saint James in 1523, during plague and famine. The first stone was laid on 21 July 1523 on land given by the Genoese nobleman António Espínola.

The chapel was repaired and blessed in 1632, then demolished and rebuilt larger by the town council between 1752 and 1768. After the 1803 flood destroyed the Calhau church, it became the parish seat, as recorded in a Latin inscription.

abstract: Short account of the few recorded capital executions in Madeira, from slaves hanged at Calheta and a friar hanged in 1582 to an English soldier hanged in 1813 during the British occupation. It also mentions an execution in effigy in the early seventeenth century.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Estreito da Calheta in western Madeira, covering the origin of its name, its early settlement by landholding families, the history of its parish church of Nossa Senhora da Graça, its chapels, localities, levadas and schools.

chapters.summary: The Elucidário finds no convincing explanation for the name Estreito. The parish grew from estates founded by André Gonçalves de França and his son João de França, who built the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça and founded an entail in 1503.
Frutuoso describes the sugar estates of João Rodrigues Castelhano and Diogo de França. Francisco Homem de Gouveia founded the chapel and entail of the Reis Magos in 1529.

The parish existed before 1562; its church was rebuilt in 1791 under Queen Maria I. The entry lists its chapels, the separation of Prazeres in 1733, water projects, localities, levadas, schools and population.

abstract: Biography of Canon Vicente Nery da Silva (d. 1860), a canon of Funchal Cathedral famed for his fiery and often aggressive preaching, author of political-ecclesiastical pamphlets and a liberal persecuted in 1828.

chapters.summary: Nery da Silva was ordained around 1815 and became a canon of Funchal Cathedral. He won great fame as a preacher but used the pulpit to attack governors and even his superiors.
He wrote thirteen polemical pamphlets, mostly printed in Funchal in 1859. As a liberal he was arrested by the 1828 alçada and sent to Lisbon.

abstract: Entry on São Pedro, the most populous of Funchal's four urban parishes, where Zargo made the first settlement; it traces the parish's creation in 1566, suppression in 1579 and restoration in 1587, its clergy stipends, church building, chapels, notable institutions and boundaries.

Stipends of the vicar, curate and beneficiaries are listed from royal charters. The seat moved from São Paulo chapel to a new church, built 1737–39 and repaired after the 1748 earthquake; Teixeira Gomes later revealed its sacristy paintings.

General survey of the island of Madeira: its position, relief, streams, towns, scenery, roads, products, fauna, minerals, irrigation, trade and industries, and the origins, physical types and customs of its population. It serves as the umbrella article introducing the more detailed 'Madeira' sub-entries.

chapters.summary: Gives Madeira's coordinates, size and distances from Porto Santo and the Desertas. Describes the central mountain range, the highest peaks, the main streams, the Funchal bay, the towns and the finest viewpoints.
Describes poor roads and transport by ox-cart, horse and hammock, the Monte railway and new motor roads. Lists crops, fauna, scarce minerals, the levadas, exports, imports and industries.

Explains that the first settlers came from Portugal, especially the Algarve, joined by foreign merchants, Spaniards, Moorish captives and African slaves. Discusses the mixed physical types still visible among Madeirans.
Describes the islanders' constitution, low crime, the old custom of brides eloping, and present prosperity. Closes by urging better roads for tourism and introducing the sub-entries.

abstract: Describes lava tubes (lava channels) in Madeira's recent basalt flows, explains how they formed, and lists examples such as the cave near the mouth of the Ribeira de São Vicente and the collapsed channel of the Fojo near Funchal.

chapters.summary: Lava tubes form when the outer crust of a lava flow cools and hardens while the molten core keeps flowing out. The best example in Madeira is a cave about 80 metres long near the mouth of the Ribeira de São Vicente.

Other tubes exist at Montado dos Pessegueiros, Porto Moniz and along the south coast near Funchal. The Fojo pit appears to be a collapsed tube, and some tubes have stalactite-like drips of glassy lava, notably at Ribeira da Janela.

abstract: The 'Hinton question' was the long political and legal controversy over the sugar and alcohol monopoly granted by the Lisbon government to the industrialist Henrique Hinton of the Torreão factory. In return he was obliged to buy south-coast sugar cane at a price fixed by law. The entry outlines the successive laws of the sugar regime from 1895 to 1920 and lists pamphlets written on the question.

abstract: Describes the stamped paper (papel selado) used for legal documents in Madeira from 1661 onwards, drawing on an article by Alberto Artur Sarmento, including its stamps, watermarks and the 'Madeira' overprints introduced because of the island's different currency.

chapters.title_pt: O papel selado no século XVII
chapters.summary: The first stamped paper used in Madeira, dated 1661, was fine linen paper with a woodcut circular stamp bearing the Portuguese arms. Later issues of 1664 and 1665 were overstamped with new dates and the provedor's signature so that they could be reused.

Until 1840 Madeiran stamped paper was the same as Portugal's, after which it carried overprints, embossed 'Tesouro Público' stamps and watermarks from Lousã. The last special paper was overprinted 'Madeira' in red because of the currency difference; all such paper came from the mainland.

abstract: Account of the one-day visit to Funchal of the President of the Republic, Dr António José de Almeida, on 9 October 1922, when he stopped on his voyage from Rio de Janeiro to Lisbon. It describes the salutes, receptions, excursions and official lunch held in his honour.

abstract: Biography of Nicolau Caetano de Bettencourt Pita (1788–1857), Funchal-born physician trained at Edinburgh, author of an early English account of Madeira and founder of the Patriota Funchalense, Madeira's first newspaper. A committed liberal, he was exiled to Terceira in 1823, where he worked as a military and civil doctor until his death.

chapters.summary: Pita was born in Funchal in 1788 and took a doctorate in medicine at Edinburgh in 1812. That year he published in London an account of Madeira's climate and geography, and in 1814 he received the privileges of Coimbra graduates.

He embraced the liberal revolution and founded the first Madeiran newspaper in 1821. After absolutism returned he was imprisoned and exiled to Terceira, where he served as a doctor and journalist until his death in 1857.

abstract: Entry on São Vicente, described as the largest and most populous parish of northern Madeira and seat of the only town on the north coast, covering its settlement, church history, localities, landscape and the deadly landslide of 1929.

chapters.summary: São Vicente became a town in the mid-18th century, a municipality in 1835 and a judicial district in 1875. The north was settled later than the south, and the parish was probably created in the last quarter of the 15th century; royal charters fixed the stipends of its vicar and curate.
An archpriesthood was based here from 1812. The parish took its name from a small hermitage of São Vicente, later enlarged in the 17th century, and has several chapels.

abstract: Account of the two bombardments of Funchal by German submarines during the First World War, on 3 December 1916 and 12 December 1917, including ships sunk, casualties, places hit and the panic among the population.

chapters.summary: A German submarine torpedoed three ships in Funchal harbour, including the French gunboat La Surprise, and then shelled the city from out of range. Deaths occurred only at sea; a monument in the Angústias cemetery commemorates the victims.

A second submarine attack lasted thirty minutes, was opposed by two armed patrol steamers and killed five people in the city. Panic led many to flee to outlying parishes, street lighting was banned until the Armistice, and an artillery company was sent to defend the island.

abstract: The Recolhimento do Bom Jesus da Ribeira in Funchal was a house of retreat for pious women founded in the 1650s by Archdeacon Simão Gonçalves Cidrão, later becoming a purely secular refuge. The entry traces its foundation, rule, finances and administration up to 1919.

chapters.summary: Archdeacon Cidrão founded the house beside the Santa Luzia stream with donations from 1655, and the first women entered in 1666. The community was exemplary, keeping choir service, but later became purely secular.

abstract: Biography of João José Xavier de Carvalhal Esmeraldo (1778–1837), 1st Count of Carvalhal, the richest landowner in Madeira, a liberal émigré in London and briefly civil governor of the archipelago in 1835.

chapters.summary: Born in Funchal in 1778, he inherited from his brother a vast collection of entailed estates, making him Madeira's richest proprietor. He lived modestly and used his fortune to relieve crises and protect poor farmers from wine merchants.

As a liberal he fled to England in 1828, supporting Madeiran exiles in London. He returned in 1834, was made count and civil governor in 1835 but soon resigned, and died at the Quinta do Palheiro in 1837.

abstract: Entry on the Pontinha, the coastal projection at the western end of Funchal bay, originally called Ilhéus after two rocky islets later joined to the shore by walls and by the breakwater (molhe) completed in 1889. chapters.summary: The site was first called Ilhéus after two rocks in the sea, later known as Pontinha. One islet was joined to the land in the 18th century and the other in 1889 by the breakwater.
The area had the Penha de França chapel and fort, and the Conceição fort on the outer islet with a chapel and a small lighthouse. The inner islet was joined to the shore in 1757–1762.
The landing quay was improved in 1850 and 1878. The Pontinha road, planned in 1872, was built slowly and later renamed several times, including rua Sacadura Cabral in 1922.

abstract: Biography of Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos (1836–1901), Funchal-born diplomat, deputy and peer, who served as Portugal's minister in Russia, translated Goethe's Faust and wrote on Columbus in Madeira.

chapters.summary: Portrait of him as a liberal-minded nobleman, born in Funchal in 1836 to a leading family. He studied law at Coimbra, graduating in 1857.
He served in Washington, Berlin, Vienna and London, then directed political affairs at the Foreign Ministry and became minister to Russia in 1894.
He was a deputy for Madeira and a peer, translated Faust, wrote his brother's biography and a memoir on Columbus, received many honours and died in Germany in 1901.

abstract: Describes the 1879 law that unified Madeira's monetary system with that of mainland Portugal, ending the circulation of foreign gold and silver coin on the island and the speculation and exchange crisis it had caused.

chapters.title_en: Foreign coin and the road to unification
chapters.title_pt: A moeda estrangeira e a proposta de unificação
chapters.summary: Foreign gold and silver coin circulated in Madeira, and Portuguese money was often refused. Finance minister Serpa Pimentel proposed unification in 1875, which became law on 2 May 1879 after lobbying by the Funchal Commercial Association and Madeiran parliamentarians.

chapters.title_en: Effects and terms of the 1879 law
chapters.summary: Unification ended abuses and a worsening exchange crisis fuelled by speculators. The law set a 1/16 discount for earlier contracts, a two-month exchange period and the minting of silver coins, while copper coin, including the pecunia madeirensis, already circulated.

abstract: Biography of Dr João Augusto Teixeira (1845–1907), a Madeiran physician, professor at the Funchal Medical-Surgical School and deputy for Madeira in 1885. The entry is largely a tribute reprinted from the newspaper Heraldo da Madeira.

chapters.summary: Teixeira was born at Ponta do Sol in 1845 and died in Funchal in 1907. He was an admired physician and an outstanding lecturer at the Medical School. He was also a fine Latinist and a prize-winning student at Coimbra.

A member of the Regenerator party, he was elected deputy in 1885 and spoke in parliament on the plight of Porto Santo. He left politics in 1901. He also held several public posts, directed the medical wards of the Santa Isabel hospital, and belonged to a family of talented men.

abstract: The Desertas are a group of three small uninhabited islands (Ilhéu Chão, Deserta Grande and Bugio) south-east of Madeira, near the Ponta de São Lourenço. The entry gives their position, distances, ecclesiastical attachment, history of ownership and sources.

chapters.summary: Describes the three islands and the Farilhão islet, their extreme points, coordinates and distances from Madeiran ports. They belong to the Sé parish, though once apparently to Caniço.

The islands were never permanently settled for lack of water, visited only for hunting, fishing and orchil gathering. They passed from the Funchal donataries to the counts of Atouguia and Taipa, were sold in 1864 and auctioned in 1894. Published sources are listed.

abstract: History of the Corpus Christi procession in Madeira from the fifteenth to the nineteenth century, covering its early burlesque character with trade guilds and figures, royal attempts to suppress profane elements, and repeated precedence disputes between the Funchal council, governors and bishops.

chapters.summary: The 1483 regulations fixed the order of trades in the Funchal procession, which had a burlesque character. Further orders followed in 1468 and 1502, and a royal decree of 1565 banned masks and profane acts.

Disputes arose over who could walk behind the canopy and carry its poles, involving vicars-general, governors and councillors, some of whom were imprisoned. Royal decrees of 1763 and earlier confirmed the council's place.

chapters.title_en: Later customs and the image of St George
chapters.summary: The procession became solemn after a 1724 royal letter removed dances and figures. A mounted image of St George accompanied it until about 1857; Ponta do Sol had its own customs, with a blacksmith playing the saint.

abstract: Survey of the Madeira archipelago as a whole: its historical importance, composition, geographical position, extreme points, area, coastline, dimensions and population, with pointers to entries on the individual islands and the Funchal district.

chapters.summary: The archipelago is praised for its natural history, wine, scenery, climate and history as Portugal's first discovery. It consists of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, lying between Europe, Morocco, the Azores and the Canaries.

The islands form a scalene triangle separated by channels of 11, 27 and 32 miles. Estimates of area vary; the 1940 census counted 251,798 inhabitants. With the Selvagens, it forms the district of Funchal.

abstract: The Lombada dos Esmeraldos, also called the Lombada da Ponta do Sol, is the great estate in Ponta do Sol parish acquired by João Esmeraldo from Rui Gonçalves da Câmara in 1473 and later divided into two entailed estates. The entry covers its history, the lawsuits over its division, its chapel of the Espírito Santo and the ruined manor house.

In 1522 Esmeraldo split the estate into two entails for his sons, leading to over a century of lawsuits. The entry describes the rich chapel of the Espírito Santo, the ruined manor house and the chapel of Santo Amaro.

abstract: Survey of the earliest printed publications in Madeira after the first press was set up in 1821, covering the first newspapers of 1821–1827 and the first pamphlets and books. It records the Statutes of the Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes (1822) as the first work printed on the island.

History of the town hall (Paços do Concelho) of Funchal: the eighteenth-century palace on Rua do Comércio bought by the municipal council in 1883, and the many buildings the council occupied from the fifteenth century onwards. It closes with brief notes on the town halls of the other Madeiran municipalities.

chapters.summary: The palace on Rua do Comércio, built in 1758 and formerly linked to the Conde de Carvalhal, passed to the firm Freitas & Macedo. The council rented it in 1868 and bought it in 1883 for 25 contos.
From orders issued in 1470 and 1486, the council first had a house on the Campo do Duque. After 1784 it moved many times between rented and owned buildings until 1862.

abstract: Entry on the small parish of Jardim do Mar on Madeira's south-west coast, covering its name, early settlers and morgados, its growth from an eighteenth-century curacy into a parish in 1848, and the Gothic-style church built by its people between 1906 and 1907.

chapters.summary: The parish takes its name from a green flat set among bare cliffs. Frutuoso's reference to it is questioned, and the early landholders, including the Couto Cardoso morgados, are named.
A curacy was created in 1734, and its chapel was rebuilt in 1786. The settlement was separated from Paul do Mar in 1836 and became a full parish in 1848.
Father César Martinho Fernandes and the parishioners, helped by Francisco João de Vasconcelos and by emigrants, built a pure Gothic church. It was blessed in 1907, and the priest died in 1920.
The entry lists the resident curates from 1837 to 1848 and describes the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade, the parish boundaries, paths and school. It ends with the barão do Jardim do Mar.

abstract: A chronological survey of noble titles granted to people connected with the Madeira archipelago, from Simão Gonçalves da Câmara's title of 1576 to nineteenth-century viscountcies and baronies. It lists each titleholder with the date of the decree where known.

chapters.summary: The earliest known title went to the captain-donatary Simão Gonçalves da Câmara in 1576. No others followed until 1812, after which titles such as Torre Bela, Porto Santo, Machico, Carvalhal, Tojal and São Pedro were granted.

Titles granted from 1851 to 1886 are listed, including Santa Cruz, Atouguia, Nogueiras, Calçada, Ribeira Brava and Orneias. Titles with unknown decree dates, and the titles of Madeira and Funchal held by governors, close the entry.

abstract: Survey of emigration from Madeira from the sixteenth century to 1916, covering the main destinations (Brazil, the British West Indies and Guiana, the United States, Hawaii, Portuguese Africa) and emigrant numbers. It shows emigration as a constant response to economic hardship and a source of remittances.

chapters.summary: Madeirans emigrated to Brazil from the sixteenth century, with government support from 1676. Passports were required from 1758 and clandestine recruiters were investigated in 1779; families also left for the United States.

chapters.title_pt: Emigração para Demerara e outros países
chapters.summary: Large-scale emigration to Demerara and the British West Indies began around 1840, and some returning emigrants became wealthy patrons of village feasts. Later currents went to Brazil, Hawaii and Portuguese Africa.
From 1903 to 1913 North America and Brazil received most Madeiran emigrants. Remittances from the United States were large, and a table gives annual totals for 1901–1916.

abstract: History and description of Funchal's municipal theatre, begun in 1884 and inaugurated in 1888, first named Teatro D. Maria Pia and renamed after Manuel de Arriaga in 1921. It lists the companies that performed there and its seating and rooms.

chapters.summary: The municipal council began the theatre in 1884 to plans by F. Soler, and it was decorated by Eugénio Cotrim and Luigi Manini. It opened in 1888 with a Spanish zarzuela, and many national and foreign companies later performed there.
The theatre's boxes, seats, atrium and upper hall are described. Its names changed from D. Maria Pia to Manuel de Arriaga, then Teatro Funchalense, and finally back to Manuel de Arriaga in 1921.

abstract: Biography of D. Luiz da Camara Leme (1817–1904), a Funchal-born general, military writer, deputy for Madeira, minister of the navy and public works, and peer of the realm, known for his long parliamentary campaign on ministerial responsibility.

chapters.summary: Camara Leme was born in Funchal in 1817 to a noble family descended from Garcia Homem de Sousa. He rose to general of division and wrote influential military works, including Elementos da Arte Militar.

He served as a deputy, including for Madeira, became a life peer in 1878 and was minister of the navy in 1870. The army honoured him with a subscription, half of which he gave to poor officers' widows; he married two actresses and died in Lisbon in 1904.

abstract: Biography of the Madeiran lawyer José Maria Martiniano da Fonseca (1794–1829), sent by governor Travassos Valdez as emissary to the liberal revolutionary junta in Porto, who was arrested and hanged there on 7 May 1829 as one of the 'Twelve Martyrs of the Fatherland'.

abstract: The Sé is the central parish of Funchal, split from the original parish of Santa Maria Maior in 1557 and seated in the cathedral; it is the city's commercial, administrative and official heart. The entry covers its creation, its curates, the churches and lost chapels within it, notable buildings and its street boundaries.

chapters.summary: The parish grew out of Santa Maria Maior and was separated in 1557, with its seat in the cathedral. Curates replaced the dean in parish duties from 1562, and their stipends were raised over time.

The parish contains several churches, the cathedral and sites of lost chapels and old buildings. It is the commercial centre with a falling population, and its limits follow streets listed in 1863; it had 4,083 inhabitants in 1921.

abstract: Account of the great forest fire of August 1919, deliberately set, which burned for eight days across much of Madeira, fanned by the dry east wind, causing losses over 2,000 contos. It lists the areas affected and those who fought the fire, and blames lenience towards arsonists for the island's deforestation.

chapters.summary: The fire began on 21 August 1919 in western Madeira and spread under a hot leste wind until rain on 28–29 August put it out, with losses over 2,000 contos.

abstract: D. Isabel de Abreu, a wealthy widow of Arco da Calheta, was twice abducted by António Gonçalves da Câmara in the sixteenth century, a dramatic episode recorded by the early chroniclers. It ended in a forced marriage, a royal inquiry and punishments.

chapters.summary: Isabel came from a noble settler family of Arco da Calheta and was the widow of the donatary's son. António Gonçalves da Câmara broke into her house to force a marriage, but she tricked him and he left for Lisbon.

Years later António seized her by force; the ouvidor of Funchal came with troops and she escaped with them. António besieged her at the Lombada da Ponta do Sol for eight days until her relatives agreed to the marriage.

Frutuoso describes the lavish wedding feast on silver plate. Her sister complained to the king, a judge punished several people, António fled but was later pardoned, and the story inspired later writings.

chapters.title_pt: Capitanias de Machico e do Funchal

abstract: The captaincy of Machico, granted by Prince Henry to Tristão Vaz in 1440, covered the north coast and eastern Madeira; the entry traces its extent, early prosperity and decline, and its troubled succession of donataries until it passed to the Crown and later holders.

chapters.title_pt: Origem, área e decadência da capitania
chapters.summary: Zarco and Tristão Vaz divided Madeira into two captaincies; Machico's charter dates from 1440. It covered the north coast and much of the east but soon declined as Funchal and Santa Cruz prospered.

Quoting Álvaro de Azevedo, the entry describes the poor rule of Tristão Vaz's descendants, the loss of the captaincy to the Crown in 1540 and its later grants. It ends with notes on ouvidores, judges and the captaincy's revenue.

abstract: Account of the royal visit of King Carlos and Queen Amélia of Portugal to Madeira from 22 to 25 June 1901, with the ceremonies, festivities and officials involved.

chapters.summary: The king and queen arrived in Funchal on 22 June 1901 with ministers and courtiers. A Te Deum was held at the cathedral and a gala reception at São Lourenço palace, followed by many festivities.

The monarchs visited barracks, charities and public buildings while the city was lavishly decorated and illuminated. They left for the Azores on 25 June, and a book by Ciriaco de Brito Nobrega describes the visit in full.
