abstract: Survey of the population of the Madeira archipelago from the first settlement to 1940, with census tables by year, municipality and parish and remarks on recurring overpopulation and emigration.

chapters.summary: Little is known about the number and origins of the first settlers, who included nobles, commoners, convicts, foreigners and many slaves. Parish registers from the later sixteenth century could allow population estimates; early figures for Porto Santo are discussed.
Tables give the archipelago's population from 1500 to 1940, the figures for its eleven municipalities and fifty parishes around 1920–1940, and the population of Funchal city from 1864 to 1930.
Overpopulation has recurred throughout Madeira's history and led to emigration, notably to British Guiana. In 1762 the governor reported people leaving for Lisbon for lack of subsistence.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Campanário, on Madeira's south coast west of Cabo Girão, explaining its name (from a bell-tower-shaped islet), its church history, early settlers, Jesuit estates and notable natives. It records the parish's move from Câmara de Lobos to the new Ribeira Brava municipality in 1914.

chapters.title_en: Origin of the name and early accounts
chapters.summary: The name comes from an islet shaped like a bell-tower, seen by the discoverers, which the sea partly destroyed in 1798. Frutuoso describes Zarco's chapel and a settlement of a hundred households given to livestock and cereals.
The parish existed before 1556, and royal charters increased the vicar's stipend. A curacy was created in 1698 and funded in 1727. The church bears the date 1683, and several chapels are listed.

Early landholders and the large Jesuit estates are described, including Fajã dos Padres with its famous Malmsey. The entry also mentions the 1625 pirate raid, the 1825 disturbances, the change of municipality in 1914, notable natives and a giant chestnut tree.
This part lists the parish's localities and schools, describes its small port and the storage caves cut into the cliff, and gives distances to nearby towns.

abstract: Surveys the protectionist legislation governing Madeira's sugar-cane and sugar industry from 1876 to 1922, including the 1904 monopoly granted to Hinton & Sons and José Júlio de Lemos and its effects on growers and consumers.

chapters.summary: Early tax exemptions for Madeiran sugar gave way to true protectionism in 1895, with minimum cane prices in exchange for privileges to factories. A 1904 law created a monopoly for two registered manufacturers, and disputes with Hinton & Sons followed.

chapters.title_pt: O decreto de 1911 e seus efeitos
chapters.summary: The 1911 decree set cane zones and prices, freed Madeiran sugar entering the mainland and regulated alcohol for wine. Growers prospered but sugar grew ever dearer in Madeira.
Sugar manufacture was declared free from 1920, with later decrees placing oversight under the 9th Region Agricultural Station. An attempt in 1922 to revive protection failed.

abstract: Entry on São Gonçalo, a suburban parish at the eastern end of Funchal, covering its territorial origins, the creation of its curacy and parish in the sixteenth century, its churches and chapels, early settlement by Gonçalo Aires, and its principal localities.

chapters.title_en: Location and creation of the parish
chapters.summary: São Gonçalo lies at the eastern edge of Funchal, between Santa Maria Maior and Caniço. Its land first belonged to Santa Maria Maior; a curacy at the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves was created in 1566, which the author considers the true founding of the parish.

A new church was ordered in 1697 because the old chapel was too small. The area was settled early, with Gonçalo Aires holding large land grants here; the entry lists chapels, the Palheiro estate, the lazaretto and the main localities, with 2,987 inhabitants in 1921.

abstract: History of the Junta Geral (district general council) of Funchal, from its creation by the laws of 1832 and 1835, through its first session in 1837, its abolition in 1892 and its restoration in 1901 under the autonomous regime.

chapters.summary: The district general councils were created in 1835, and the Madeira council held its first ordinary session in 1837 with twelve members. Later administrative codes changed the number of members and the method of election.
The councils were abolished in 1892, but Funchal's was restored in 1901 under the special Azorean-style autonomous regime. The 1913 law set its composition by municipality.

abstract: General survey of the animal life of the Madeira archipelago: its European origin, endemism, the numbers of species by group, birds, invertebrates and marine fishes, and the naturalists who studied it.

chapters.title_en: Origins and composition of the fauna
chapters.summary: Madeira's fauna came from Europe, carried by birds, winds and sea currents, and it has no native land mammals except the monk seal. More than 3,100 animal species are known, and many land snails and insects are endemic.

About 200 bird species have been recorded, including endemic forms, and there are around 250 fish species, notably tuna and black scabbardfish. The entry ends with a list of naturalists who studied the fauna.

chapters.title_pt: Origem flamenga e vinda à Madeira
chapters.summary: The Lemes descend from Flemish nobles of Bruges who fought for Portugal at Arzila and Tangier and received arms in 1471. Martim de Leme settled in Madeira around 1483 with land grants in Santo António, where the family built the Quinta do Leme and its chapel.

chapters.title_en: The Leme entail and its holders
chapters.summary: Pedro de Leme founded the entail, but he and his son died in prison in Lisbon in 1556. The entail passed through lawsuits and several heirs of the Câmara Leme line until it was absorbed by the house of Carvalhal.
The entry quotes a genealogical source stating that the Câmara Lemes never had a right to 'Dom', and recounts a story that it arose from a clerk misreading an abbreviation.

abstract: Entry on the German volcanologist Alphons Stuebel of Dresden, who studied Madeira in 1862–63 and built a relief geological map of the island now kept in the Funchal Seminary Museum; it reproduces, via Father Ernesto Schmitz, his view that Madeira was formed by two linked eruptive centres, the Curral das Freiras caldera and the Paul da Serra dome.

chapters.title_en: Stuebel and his relief map of Madeira
chapters.title_pt: Stuebel e o seu mapa em relevo
chapters.summary: The article supplements the geology entry with Father Schmitz's account of Stuebel. Stuebel studied Madeira in 1862–63 and built a relief geological map, now in the Seminary Museum in Funchal, and set out his views in works on Ecuador's volcanoes.

Stuebel argues that Madeira's mountains came from two simultaneous eruptive centres: the Curral das Freiras caldera and the flattened dome of Paul da Serra. The São Vicente and Ribeira Brava valleys mark the boundary and are erosional, not craters.

He notes small preserved craters, such as the lagoon of the Serra de Santo António and cones above Porto Moniz, and says Madeira first suggested his theories of volcanism. He compares Madeira with Tenerife, also formed of two joined parts.

abstract: Biography of Tristão Vaz, companion of João Gonçalves Zargo in the discovery of Madeira and first captain-donatary of Machico. It argues that he never bore the surname Teixeira, which came to his descendants from his wife Branca Teixeira.

chapters.title_en: The question of the surname Teixeira
chapters.summary: The entry argues that Tristão Vaz was never called Teixeira. The name came from his wife Branca Teixeira and was later used by his descendants, and it was wrongly given to him by later chroniclers.
Documents show he was a noble squire of Prince Henry's household, known simply as 'Tristão da Ilha', with a phoenix in his arms. Zargo, however, was held to rank above him.

Born in the late fourteenth century, he fought in Africa and settled in Madeira in 1425. He was exiled to São Tomé for punishing Diogo Barradas but later restored, and he died at Silves aged over eighty.

abstract: Biography of João Fernandes Vieira (born Francisco de Ornelas Moniz), a Madeiran from Machico who emigrated to Brazil and led the Portuguese restoration of Pernambuco against the Dutch. The entry also discusses his baptismal record in Faial and the monument to him in Funchal.

chapters.summary: Vieira was born in the captaincy of Machico to impoverished noble families. Like many younger sons of decayed morgados, he emigrated to Brazil under an assumed name.

As a clerk in Pernambuco he fought the Dutch invaders from 1630, was captured, later married and grew rich, and then led the revolt that expelled the Dutch. He became governor of Paraíba and Angola and died in Olinda in 1681.
The entry lists works on Vieira and cites a Faial baptismal record suggesting he was born in 1596. A monument to him was inaugurated in Funchal in 1924 and moved to the Jardim Municipal in 1933.

abstract: Biography of José Silvestre Ribeiro (1807–1891), civil governor of Funchal from 1846 to 1852, regarded by the Elucidário as the most distinguished and beneficent governor Madeira ever had. It lists his many public works and reforms and the honours he received.

chapters.summary: Ribeiro was born in 1807, trained in law and fought in the liberal army. He later held high public offices. He came to Madeira in 1846 with the royal commissioner Avila after the Kalley religious disturbances and became civil governor.

The chapter lists his main achievements, including the Asylum, famine relief, public lighting, schools, levadas and the Ponte Monumental. It also covers his years as a deputy, the gold collar given to him by Madeirans, and his earlier work rebuilding Praia da Vitória.

The Azores marked his centenary in 1907, but Madeira did not. In Funchal a street bears his name, and the chapter lists sources on his administration. He lost his only son in Funchal, left Madeira in 1852 and died in Lisbon in 1891.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Santa Cruz, one of Madeira's oldest settlements, named after a cross Zarco had raised there at the discovery; it covers its early ecclesiastical history, collegiate church, chapels, noble settlers and localities.

chapters.summary: Verse and chronicle accounts tell how Zarco had a cross made from old tree trunks, giving Santa Cruz its name. The parish grew quickly, rivalled Machico, and was probably created in the second quarter of the 15th century.

Royal charters set the stipends of the vicar, curate, beneficiaries, preacher and organist. The large three-aisled church of São Salvador was built in 1533 under João de Freitas, and many chapels existed or have vanished.
Noble settlers founded entailed houses, and the Freitas family distinguished itself in Asia. The entry ends with the parish's localities and its 1921 population of 7,054.

abstract: History of the Funchal Beggars' Asylum, founded in March 1847 by civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro during the famine of 1846–47 and later merged with an orphan asylum. The entry follows its successive premises, the history of the Casa das Angústias building, and its main benefactors.

chapters.title_pt: A fome e a fundação do asilo
chapters.summary: The famine of 1846–47 filled Funchal's streets with beggars. Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro gathered them into a warehouse in March 1847 and then moved about 400 inmates to the former convent of São Francisco, appointing an administrative committee.
The asylum moved in December 1847 to the Casa das Angústias, built by the council in 1837, which had meanwhile housed the town hall and other offices. The council's cession became definitive in 1913.

After the 1856 cholera epidemic an orphan asylum was created and merged with the beggars' asylum in 1862. Governor Jacinto António Perdigão gave it statutes and a permanent fund, and the Countess of Ribeiro Real later left it the Quinta Esmeraldo.

chapters.summary: News of the revolution reached Funchal in late 1640 and early January 1641. On 11 January the governor, bishop and council acclaimed João IV, and the Castilian garrison did not resist.

abstract: Biographical and bibliographical entry on Baltazar Dias, a blind sixteenth-century Madeiran poet, reputedly from Santana, whose popular religious and secular autos were reprinted for centuries. abstract: Transcribes the views of agricultural regent José Cruz Tavares on expanding vineyards on Porto Santo, whose grapes and musts suit table wine, fresh fruit, raisins and the sweetening of Madeira's fortified wines. chapters.summary: The editors introduce Tavares's articles. He argues that the vine grows best in Porto Santo's poor soil, supports its 2,500 farmers, and could help cover the treeless, drought-prone island.

chapters.summary: About 250,000 kg of grapes are produced, mostly made into must for table wine or for exporters' fortified wines. Porto Santo table wine could replace imported mainland wine, and the fresh grape trade needs regulation.

abstract: Survey of the use of irrigation water in Madeira from settlement onwards, covering the building of levadas, the royal charters regulating water rights from the fifteenth century, and the State's later role in constructing levadas.

abstract: Account of the two cholera epidemics in Madeira: the catastrophic outbreak of July–October 1856, brought by an infantry regiment from Lisbon and officially killing 7,041 people (reputedly about 10,000), and the far milder epidemic of 1910–1911, which killed 556 under the direction of Dr Carlos França.

chapters.title_en: Arrival and spread of cholera in 1856
chapters.summary: Cholera arrived with Infantry Regiment No. 1 from Lisbon in June 1856 and spread from Funchal across the island. Rural parishes suffered from hunger and a lack of doctors, and the parish death tolls are listed.
The civil governor and Dr António da Luz Pita organised relief, and medicines, bedding and money came from Lisbon. Several doctors died, and further reading is suggested.

A milder outbreak began in October 1910. A high commissioner and Dr Carlos França were sent from Lisbon, and França directed the sanitary services. Deaths totalled 556, and the north coast and Calheta were largely spared.

As deputy for Madeira from 1900 to 1910 he pressed for the completion of the levadas, proposed the first autonomy bill, and secured a loan for Funchal's water and sewerage works and a telephone network.
He taught at the Funchal lyceum, wrote for local newspapers and served the Progressive Party led by his father-in-law; he left politics after the Republic and died in Funchal in 1915.

abstract: D. Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão was the 17th bishop of Funchal (1757–1784). He reformed clerical and convent discipline, briefly served as governor of Madeira, and was criticised for his pastoral letter against the expelled Jesuits.

chapters.summary: Brandão led the diocese of Funchal for 26 years, and his harsh stance on the expulsion of the Jesuits was criticised. He was born at Vila Cova de Sub Avo and was appointed bishop in 1756. He arrived in Funchal on 5 August 1757.

Helped by the missionaries Alasia and Reis, he reformed the convents, the seminary and the clergy. He governed the archipelago in 1758–59 and later clashed with Governor Câmara Coutinho over an imprisonment. He died in Funchal in 1784 and was buried in the cathedral.

abstract: Entry on the sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas), a staple food of rural Madeirans, covering its introduction to the island, cultivation, varieties and local names of its vines, and uses as food and fodder.

chapters.summary: The sweet potato came from South America; the cut-leaved form reached Madeira in the mid-17th century and the entire-leaved form in 1845 from Demerara. It is propagated from cuttings and yields one to three harvests a year depending on altitude.

Two varieties, cordifolia and digitata, are grown, with many named sub-varieties of 'rama'. The tubers feed people and animals, the vines are good fodder, and the crop is grown in furrows alongside other plants.

abstract: Account of the Junta Autónoma das Obras do Porto do Funchal, the autonomous board created in 1913 to improve Funchal harbour, covering its remit, membership, revenues, projects, the failed Fumasil contract and works carried out around 1930–33.

chapters.summary: The board was created by decree in 1913 to repair the Pontinha breakwater, build quays, a customs link and other harbour facilities. Its members were local officials and elected representatives, and its revenues came from surcharges and taxes.
Successive harbour projects by Furtado de Mendonça and Francisco Soares Júnior are described, along with an earlier 1911 commission whose engineer Adriano Trigo wrote a study.

After a failed contract with the Fumasil Company, rescinded in 1928, the board reinforced the Pontinha breakwater and extended the city quay in 1930–33. Tobacco import tax revenues, staff and a bibliography follow.

abstract: Account of the two British military occupations of Madeira during the Napoleonic Wars, in 1801–1802 and 1807–1814, and of the Portuguese diplomatic efforts to end them.

chapters.summary: A British squadron landed about 3,500 troops at Funchal in July 1801, officially to protect the island from France. The governor gave way to avoid bombardment, and Portugal protested in London. The troops left in January 1802.

In December 1807 Admiral Hood and General Beresford took Madeira by capitulation. Diplomacy by Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho restored civil government to Portugal in 1808, but British troops stayed until October 1814.

Describes the successive official boundaries of the city of Funchal, from the limits fixed in 1809 through the alvará of 1863 and the municipal ordinance of 1909 to the much enlarged perimeter adopted in 1927.

chapters.summary: The 1909 ordinance defined the urban area by six vertices. Earlier limits were set by the alvará of 1863 and by a council commission in 1809.

The city grew after the 1803 flood. In 1927 the council nearly doubled its area to take in suburban parishes, although residents still regarded the 1909 limits as the real city. The 1920 census gave 24,284 inhabitants.

abstract: Biography of José António Monteiro Teixeira (1795–1876), Funchal-born poet educated in France, French consul in Madeira and satirical poet writing in Portuguese and French.

chapters.summary: Born in Funchal in 1795 to a wealthy family, he was sent at twelve to a college in Pau, France, at his mother's insistence. His parents had no news of him for two years because of the Napoleonic wars.
He stayed in Paris and visited London, befriending Chateaubriand, Béranger, Méry, Barthélemy, Castilho and others.
Back in Madeira he served as French consul and Funchal councillor, refusing honours; France gave him a gold medal after the 1840 Belle Poule visit.
He wrote epigrams and satire after Tolentino, and French verse, publishing several volumes between 1848 and 1871. He died in Funchal in 1876.

abstract: Entry on the parish of Santa Maria Maior, in the eastern part of Funchal, the oldest parish of the archipelago, also known as Nossa Senhora do Calhau or the Socorro parish. It covers the origin of its names, the moves of its parish seat, its clergy and collegiate body, its chapels, landmarks, population and disputed boundaries.

chapters.summary: The parish lies on the eastern side of Funchal. Its names (Santa Maria Maior, Conceição de Baixo, Nossa Senhora do Calhau, Socorro) come from its church and the image venerated there. It was the first and is the oldest parish of the archipelago.

The seat moved to the Cathedral around 1508, and the parish was split in 1557. The entry lists its early priests, the stipend of the first vicar, the creation of its curacy and collegiate body, and its chapels.

The parish contains squares, the São Tiago fortress and industrial sites. It had 7,823 inhabitants in 1921, and its customary boundaries with São Gonçalo differ from those in the official street map of 1863.

abstract: Biography of Conselheiro José Leite Monteiro (1841–1920), a Porto-born jurist, journalist and philosophy teacher at the Funchal lyceum who served as acting civil governor and president of the Funchal municipal council and the Junta Geral.

chapters.summary: Although not Madeiran, Leite Monteiro was devoted to the island and was a gifted but modest jurist. He was born in Porto in 1841, the son of a judge who served in Funchal.
He studied law at Coimbra, published controversial early works and wrote widely for Funchal newspapers. His legal work as an advocate was largely left unpublished.

He won the post of philosophy teacher at the Funchal lyceum in 1867 and held high local offices, promoting the public library. He was active in party politics, co-edited Flores da Madeira and died in 1920.

abstract: Entry on the upland parish of Santo António da Serra (Santo da Serra), on a plateau above Santa Cruz and Machico, covering its settlement, ecclesiastical history, church, Protestant troubles and the short-lived Aldeia da Rainha colony of Porto Santo settlers.

chapters.summary: The parish lies on a plateau at about 700 m and is a favoured summer resort. Land clearing began in the 16th century and Gil de Carvalho built early chapels.
Disputes among neighbouring vicars led the bishop to take the chapel under his protection in 1612; a curacy was created in 1813 and an autonomous parish in 1848.

The church was rebuilt in the 1850s, largely at the expense of the American consul John Howard March, and blessed in 1857. The entry also notes a pilgrims' house, a bishop's exile and Kalley's Protestant preaching.
Queen Maria I settled poor Porto Santo islanders here as the Aldeia da Rainha, but they abandoned it by 1783. The entry ends with the parish's localities and population.

abstract: A chronology of the floods (aluviões) that struck Madeira from the seventeenth century to 1921, above all the catastrophic flood of 9 October 1803 that destroyed much of Funchal and killed about six hundred people. It records damage, casualties and the official responses, including the channelling of Funchal's streams.

chapters.title_en: Introduction and the floods of 1724 and 1765
chapters.summary: Floods were known before 1724. The 1724 flood devastated Machico, and in 1765 the Ponte da Praça in Funchal was destroyed.

The 1803 flood was the worst disaster in the island's history, destroying the Santa Maria Maior district and its church and killing around 600 people. The governor provided relief and Oudinot was sent to wall in Funchal's streams.

The 1815 flood caused great damage in Funchal, especially along the São João stream. The 1842 flood inundated the city, followed by a storm that wrecked boats in the harbour; floods in 1848 hit Santana.
Floods and storms in 1856, 1876, 1895, 1901, 1920 and 1921 caused damage across the island. Earlier floods of 1611 and 1707 are also noted.

abstract: Describes the Madeiran cereal regime, the legal monopoly on the import and trade of wheat and flour established in 1899, and the laws that modified and finally ended it in the early 1920s. abstract: History of the government plant nursery (viveiro) founded in 1799 at the Lombada, Monte parish, which distributed over 20,000 trees across Madeira and Porto Santo before its abolition in 1828, together with later unrealised plans for nurseries and acclimatisation gardens in Funchal.

abstract: Biography of D. Jerónimo Barreto (1543–1589), sixth bishop of Funchal (1574–1585), remembered chiefly for convening the island's first diocesan synod and promulgating the Diocesan Constitutions of 1578.

chapters.summary: Barreto, of noble birth near Braga, studied theology at Coimbra and was named bishop of Madeira in 1572, being consecrated in 1573 once he reached canonical age.

Arriving in 1574, he held Madeira's first diocesan synod and promulgated the Diocesan Constitutions in 1578, created parishes and reformed the chapter. He was moved to the Algarve in 1585 and died there in 1589.

abstract: The braguinha is a small four-stringed guitar-like instrument peculiar to Madeira, played chiefly by country people in popular ensembles; the entry describes its tuning, playing technique, teachers, its spread by emigrants to Hawaii, and the possible origins of its alternative names.

chapters.summary: The braguinha is a small wooden guitar with 17 frets and four gut strings tuned D, G, B, D. It has a bright, lively sound, is played mostly by ordinary people with the thumb, and accompanies or leads popular ensembles.

Funchal had several braguinha teachers, and Agostinho Martins led an orchestra of braguinhas, rajões and violas. Emigrants took the instrument to Hawaii; its names machete de braga and braga may derive from old breeches called bragas.

abstract: History of public street lighting in Funchal, from a short-lived attempt in 1821 and José Silvestre Ribeiro's oil lamps of 1846, through petroleum lighting and failed gas projects, to the electric lighting inaugurated in 1897.

abstract: History of Funchal's industrial (later industrial and commercial) school, from the drawing and painting class founded in 1809 through its creation as the Josefa de Óbidos industrial drawing school in 1889, its renaming, reforms, teachers, directors, courses and enrolment up to 1941.

abstract: Entry on the small north-coast parish of Arco de São Jorge, between São Jorge and Boaventura, created in 1676. It covers its church history, fertility and climate, the remarkable landslide of 1689 that formed the Quebrada, and notable natives.

chapters.summary: The parish took its name from the surrounding hills and split from São Jorge in 1676. Its seat was the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade, replaced by a new church blessed in 1744.
The parish is very fertile but short of irrigation water; a planned levada was never built. Its climate is mild, though epidemics struck in 1768 and 1849.
A great landslide on Easter night 1689 carried land into the sea almost intact, as described in a contemporary letter.
Notable natives and residents are described, together with the patron saint, pious bequests and the parish's low illiteracy. It lies in Santana municipality and has 167 inhabitants.

abstract: Account, drawn mainly from Frutuoso's Saudades da Terra, of the 1533 episode in Porto Santo when Fernão Nunes 'o Bravo' and his niece Filipa Nunes posed as prophets, gaining the credence of people, officials and clergy until the corregedor arrested them. It records the killing of the notary João Calaça, the sentences imposed in Évora and the fine levied on the islanders.

chapters.summary: In 1533 Fernão Nunes came down from the hills claiming the Holy Spirit had sent him to preach with his paralysed niece Filipa. The people, officials and clergy believed him, and a notary who read a prayer book during a sermon was killed by the crowd.
The population neglected their work and followed the prophet's strange orders, including sending a couple half-naked to a chapel in winter. Priests even named him in the Mass.

The corregedor João de Afonseca arrested the prophets and the clergy and sent the inquiry to the King. The prophets did public penance at Évora cathedral, the islanders were fined 200 cruzados, and a later book credits Friar Gaspar Gato with exposing the fraud.
